title: Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers preview: 4 key stats
summary: This will be the third meeting between the Lions and Panthers in the Dan Campbell era and the first in primetime. Neither of the previous two matchups was decided by fewer than two touchdowns, and Dave Canales, hosting his first primetime game at the helm, will already be the third different Panthers head coach Detroit […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 24: Detroit Lions offensive tackle Penei Sewell (58) during an NFL football game between the Detroit Lions and the Carolina Panthers on December 24, 2022, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Ic on Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images This will be the third meeting between the Lions and Panthers in the Dan Campbell era and the first in primetime. Neither of the previous two matchups was decided by fewer than two touchdowns, and Dave Canales, hosting his first primetime game at the helm, will already be the third different Panthers head coach Detroit has faced during that span. The Panthers may sit at only 1-2, with losses to the Bears and Browns, but they’ve seen some improved play early from to-be-determined franchise quarterback Bryce Young, Jameson Williams’ former quarterback at Alabama, and cannot be taken lightly. After all, Carolina has more recently made the postseason and won its division than Detroit. The Panthers have finished top five in total free-agent guarantees handed out to defensive players in each of the past two offseasons, committing more than $225 million guaranteed to defensive additions over that span. Yet, despite all that spending and being under the siege of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero, they’re still playing like a bottom-10 unit. The Lions, already playing their second road primetime game of the season, will look to reverse their fortunes from Buffalo and potentially put together their most complete performance yet during Alim McNeill’s homecoming. While some rain is expected, much of the analysis consists of passing statistics given the tendencies and personnel of both teams. With that, let’s get into my four key stats and matchups for Sunday night’s game. Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus. Cheaper By the Dozen The Panthers, in Year 4 of Young, made the switch from head coach Dave Canales to offensive coordinator Brad Idzik as the primary offensive playcaller and have placed more of the load on Young’s shoulders. They’ve had success against the Bears and Falcons defenses but struggled against the Browns. Through three weeks, the Panthers’ 67.9% pass rate ranks third-highest in the league, with Young leading the NFL at 313 passing yards per game. He’ll face a Lions pass defense that ranks dead last with 299.3 passing yards allowed per game, 27th at +0.16 EPA/pass, and 24th with a 48.5% pass success rate allowed. The Panthers have had even more passing success when they go to 12-personnel, mixing in combinations of Darren Waller, Tommy Tremble, and Mitchell Evans to go along with Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker at wide receiver. This season, passing from 12-personnel, the Panthers are 20-for-27, a 74.1% completion percentage (8th), for 317 passing yards (2nd) and 11.7 yards per attempt (2nd), with strong analytical metrics as well: a 10.76-yard aDOT (5th), 63.0% success rate (4th), and +0.35 EPA/play (7th). The Panthers’ pressure rate allowed, which overall sits at 52.6% and ranks last in the NFL, drops to only 40.7% (20th) when passing out of 12-personnel. It’s been an added element that Idzik has brought to their offense this season after they didn’t have nearly as much reliance or success with it last year. The most common targets for Young when passing from 12-personnel have been Tremble (8 targets, 6 catches, 61 receiving yards), Coker (4 targets, 4 catches, 106 receiving yards), McMillan (5 targets, 3 catches, 62 receiving yards), and Waller (3 targets, 3 catches, 43 receiving yards). It’s a potent condensed passing attack for the Detroit Lions to defend. The Lions defense, which has prided itself on its preference for base defense throughout the majority of the Dan Campbell era—running more of it than anyone last season—has been worked as a pass defense this season, both overall and specifically against 12-personnel. The Lions pass defense has been getting shredded against 12-personnel: 33 dropbacks (30th, 3rd most) 29 pass attempts (30th) 21 completions (31st) 291 passing yards (32nd) 72.4% completion percentage (26th) 8.8 yards per pass (25th) 4 passing touchdowns (t-31st) 8.41 aDOT (21st) 55.2% passing success rate (19th) +0.38 EPA per play (25th) Teams have given the Lions a heavy dose of 12-personnel, and they haven’t had answers, all while the Lions’ pressure rate and sack rate are also lower against 12-personnel than they are overall. Kelvin Sheppard will need to equip his defense with better answers against the Panthers. And while the Lions’ cornerback group has been much maligned, having success in coverage against Carolina’s 12-personnel passing attack will also be reliant on improvement from the spine of the defense, with linebackers Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and perhaps Trevor Nowaske or Malcolm Rodriguez, along with safeties Chuck Clark and Christian Izien, needing to execute better. Young and the Restless The one area where the Panthers’ passing offense has faltered, as mentioned in the last section, is allowing a league-high pressure rate. Much like Jared Goff and his elite-level processing skills have continued to pick apart the blitz, Bryce Young has found a higher level of success against the blitz so far this season. When defenses don’t bring those additional pass rushers, however, that’s where the Panthers’ prowling passing attack has been declawed. The Panthers’ yards per pass drop from 8.3 (4th) against the blitz to 6.1 (18th) with no blitz, while their EPA per pass plummets from +0.35 (6th) to -0.09 (21st). Not only does the passing production drop, but the heat applied to Young actually increases. Against the blitz, the Panthers’ pressure rate is 39.5% (t-11th) and their sack rate is only 2.3% (5th). With no blitz, their pressure rate climbs to 45.3% (32nd), while their sack rate jumps to 7.0% (21st). Young and the offense operate more efficiently when he’s sped up and can attack the vacancies left behind in coverage. The Detroit Lions’ defensive front has shown some teeth early this season, generating a 36.8% pressure rate (3rd) and 6.9% sack rate (12th) when not blitzing. The Panthers were already dealing with backup offensive tackles in Rasheed Walker and rookie Monroe Freeling, and with the injury to left guard Damien Lewis, they’ll be left to play 2024 UDFA Corey Bullock and his 55 career offensive snaps in the first start of his career. It could be the perfect recipe for disaster for Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, and company to maul the Panthers and leave their passing offense to die in the wilderness—if the coverage behind them can hold up. It’ll also be on Kelvin Sheppard to calculatedly call off the dogs, rush four, and ask questions later. Lion Kings of the Jungle The Carolina Panthers are playing light boxes (six or fewer defenders) on a league-high 40.2% of plays. While defensive tackle Derrick Brown is an imposing player in the middle, the Panthers have been leaving prized free-agent signing Devin Lloyd and Bobby Okereke—a player exposed by Jahmyr Gibbs against the Giants last season—out to dry in the run defense this season. They’re also relying on undrafted rookie Aaron Hall and fellow rookie Lee Hunter as the two defensive tackles trying to hold down the fort next to Brown on the interior. Against Man/Duo run concepts, the Panthers have allowed 132 rushing yards on 16 carries and rank league-worst in all of the following: 8.3 yards per carry, four rushing touchdowns, and +0.45 EPA per rush. Meanwhile, on such runs this season, Gibbs has 12 carries for 61 rushing yards (5.1 yards per carry) and a rushing touchdown, along with an impressive 58.3% rushing success rate. Look for the Lions to go big-on-big, take advantage of the light boxes, and allow Penei Sewell and the re-engineered Detroit People Movers to mash bodies and control the line of scrimmage, giving Gibbs downhill running room…

title: 5 things we learned from Dan Campbell in Week 4
summary: On Friday morning, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke for the third and last time before the team’s Week 4 game against the Carolina Panthers. Fridays tend to be a news dump, and this week was no exception. Campbell led off by announcing that the team was very much involved in trade talks for Joey […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday August 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co On Friday morning, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell spoke for the third and last time before the team’s Week 4 game against the Carolina Panthers. Fridays tend to be a news dump, and this week was no exception. Campbell led off by announcing that the team was very much involved in trade talks for Joey Porter Jr. , and that Lions safety Brian Branch is very close to returning to practice . Here are five other things we learned from Campbell on Friday. Jack Campbell is ‘fine’ Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell would be the first to tell you that his start to the season isn’t what he thought it would be. His coverage has been off, he hasn’t been a noticeable force in the run game, and something has felt off through three games. But Dan Campbell expressed zero loss of faith in his linebacker. “Jack’s not gone,” Campbell said. “I mean, I get it, and he holds himself to high standards just like we all do. We want to be better in all areas, but Jack’s just fine. He’ll be just fine. And look, Jack’s the guy who just got paid and he’s going to be worried about getting cut every freaking week. I mean, that’s Jack, that’s his mentality. And more importantly, letting his teammates down; that means something to him. So he works every day and he works his craft every day. He doesn’t go in the tank or lose confidence. He just continues to go. So, he’s our bell cow and he’ll be fine. He’s going to be just fine.” Containing Bryce Young in the pocket is a high priority All week, Campbell has talked about how the defense’s game plan this week revolves around Panthers quarterback Bryce Young and containing the young passer from explosive plays. That involves keeping Young in the pocket and not letting him beat you with his feet. Oddly enough, though, Young only has three rushes on the season, as his focus has been maneuvering in the pocket to find a play downfield. I asked Campbell if he was surprised Young has only rushed three times this year, and the Lions coach admitted he was—but that won’t stop the team from focusing on his feet. “I am because that’s been something that he’s done quite a bit of and really hurts defenses,” Campbell said. “So I am, but no matter what it is, his eyes are always downfield. And then it’s, ‘Okay, well it’s not there. I’m out in the open. I’ll take off.’ “So, he’s still dangerous. It still shows up. I mean, he had one in Chicago Week 1 that was — there it is, man. You just gave him the lane. Everybody’s covered up and then he takes it all the way. So I am, but that whole thing doesn’t mean anything because I’m like, we better be ready. I mean, he could take off 10 times this game for all I know if we give it to him.” Tight ends defense remains a concern Thus far, the Lions have been extremely leaky when it comes to defending tight ends. Through three games, they’ve allowed 351 receiving yards (32nd) and six touchdowns (32nd) to tight ends . The Panthers bolster a decent trio of tight ends in Tommy Tremble (seven catches, 70 yards), Mitchell Evans (five catches, 58 yards), and Darren Waller (10 catches, 112 yards, 2 TDs), and Campbell says they are all dangerous. “Anytime that you have versatile tight ends that can do everything for you because they’ve got kind of the perfect blend of what they can do,” Campbell said. Waller is their guy, get down the field, vertical threat, range. (Tremble can do it all, and so can (Mitchell Evans) 84, for that matter, but he’s relied on a little bit more in the blocking in line stuff. But all three of those guys, when you have the versatility, you can do a lot of different jobs, a lot of different schemes. And so look, it’s something we’re aware of.” Rookie LB Jimmy Rolder may get some defensive playing time Jimmy Rolder made his NFL debut last week against the New York Jets, but exclusively played on special teams (15 snaps). Campbell noted that they are considering giving him a defensive role. “We got one sample size of him, and that looked good on special teams. Is that here to stay? Do you continue to get better? We’d like to mix him in at times if we could this game on some defense, but we’ll see where that’s at,” Campbell said. Rolder got off to a hot start in training camp, regularly working with the second-team defense. However, his progress was stopped before the pads even came on when he suffered a leg injury that held him out for the remainder of training camp. Now, with a full month of practice under his belt, it’s possible we see what the former Wolverine has to offer. Dan Campbell’s been dying for someone like DJ Wonnum For years, the Detroit Lions have been trying to find some sort of complement to Aidan Hutchinson on the other side of the defensive line. And it appears they finally got the player they want in DJ Wonnum. Campbell said they were “dying for” a player like him because he’s such a perfect fit. “Man, he’s kind of this lunch pail guy at the defensive end. He does everything right,” Campbell said. “There’s nothing flashy yet. Man, he’s pretty crafty, and he’s pretty smooth, but he can be violent on the edge. It’s so consistent, and that’s exactly what we acquired. I love the consistency.” Last week, Wonnum notched 2.0 sacks against the Jets, and Campbell believes it’s only a matter of time before Wonnum’s wins begin to trickle down to the rest of the defensive line. “It started to come to life here. He’s getting his own wins over there opposite of Hutch. They’re using a lot of resources over there against 97 and man, now he’s starting to show up over there,” Campbell said. “Now they got to decide, alright, are we going to help there too a little bit? And now you’re opening up for (Lions DL Alim McNeill) Mac and (Lions DL Skyler Gill-Howard) Sky and those guys in the middle and (Lions DL) Tyleik (Williams).”

title: Detroit Lions injury update: Brian Branch nearly ready to return
summary: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch is apparently very close to returning to practice. After suffering a torn Achilles in early December last year, the All-Pro safety could show up in practice at any time. “He’s close. Yep, he’s close,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Friday morning. “He’s ready to go. [I’m] tired of listening […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - DECEMBER 4: Brian Branch #32 of the Detroit Lions stretches prior to an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Ford Field on December 04, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch is apparently very close to returning to practice. After suffering a torn Achilles in early December last year, the All-Pro safety could show up in practice at any time. “He’s close. Yep, he’s close,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Friday morning. “He’s ready to go. [I’m] tired of listening to him. So, I mean that in a good way. Man, he’s put in a ton of work, and he looks really good. He’s close.” Branch is eligible to return to practice at any time thanks to a new rule regarding the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Branch is not eligible to play until after this weekend’s game against the Carolina Panthers, but he could theoretically return to action next week against the Arizona Cardinals. Detroit does have a Week 6 bye, so perhaps the team’s Week 7 game against the Green Bay Packers is a more realistic target date. Once the Lions opt to return Branch to practice, they have a 21-day window to put him back on the 53-man roster, activating him from the PUP list. In the meantime, the Lions have been making do at the safety position. With Kerby Joseph also still on PUP and Avonte Maddox out for the year with a foot injury, Detroit has relied upon veteran Chuck Clark and fourth-year defensive back Christian Izien. In three seasons with Detroit, Branch has 258 tackles, 20 tackles for loss, 38 passes defended, seven interceptions, and three forced fumbles.

title: Dan Campbell admits Detroit Lions had significant interest in Joey Porter Jr.
summary: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell confirmed several reports that the team was in on trade discussions with the Pittsburgh Steelers regarding Joey Porter Jr. The young cornerback was traded this week to the Dallas Cowboys for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick. But Campbell said that general manager Brad Holmes was active […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JULY 29: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions speaks during a press conference during Detroit Lions Training Camp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell confirmed several reports that the team was in on trade discussions with the Pittsburgh Steelers regarding Joey Porter Jr. The young cornerback was traded this week to the Dallas Cowboys for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick. But Campbell said that general manager Brad Holmes was active in those talks as well. “Brad was, he’s been on it for a while,” Campbell said. “That’s been ongoing, and everything’s got to align right, you know. The Cowboys did what they wanted to do, but we were very much in on it.” The Lions certainly appear to have a need at cornerback. Detroit ranks at or near the bottom of the league in pass defense stats, including yards allowed (32nd), passer rating (27th), and success rate (29th). Detroit has already benched Rock Ya-Sin for both Roger McCreary and Ennis Rakestraw after cutting Terrion Arnold this offseason. Campbell was asked if the team is still active in discussions to acquire more cornerback talent on the market, and the Lions coach gave a boilerplate answer about how the team is always looking. “Just like any year, it’s non-stop,” Campbell said. “Brad’s constantly looking to upgrade this roster at every position. If we can find somebody that we feel like fits us and can help us and the value is right, we will.” It’s not very often that the Lions openly talk about their interest in a player on the trade block, so this does lend credence to Detroit’s true interest in upgrading the cornerback room. But until they actually acquire a player, they will likely continue to receive criticism for what appears to be the team’s biggest weakness.

title: Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The Detroit Lions and Carolina Panthers face off on Sunday night in a litmus test game for both franchises. Though the Panthers are 1-2 and the Lions are 2-1, both teams are very much considered a competitor for their respective divisions, and both are looking for a defining win to silence some of the doubters. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 8: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions hugs Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers after the game at Ford Field on October 8, 2023 in Detroit, Michigan. The Lions beat the Panthers 42-24. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions and Carolina Panthers face off on Sunday night in a litmus test game for both franchises. Though the Panthers are 1-2 and the Lions are 2-1, both teams are very much considered a competitor for their respective divisions, and both are looking for a defining win to silence some of the doubters. The Lions are currently 3.5-point favorites according to FanDuel Sportsbook, but this one could be even closer than that. Let’s break down the matchup in this week’s On Paper statistical breakdown, preview, and prediction of Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers Note: We are throwing away all 2025 data. Everything listed below represents 2026 only, unless otherwise stated. Lions pass offense (12th) vs. Panthers pass defense (16th) Through the first three weeks of the season, I expressed a healthy amount of optimism for the Lions’ passing attack given the incredible consistency they’ve shown over the last three years. They’ve rewarded that trust with one of the most efficient passing attacks in football thus far. Through three weeks, the Lions rank: Third in passer rating (116.1) 10th in yards per attempt (7.4) Sixth in dropback EPA (0.286) Fifth in success rate (53.2%) Behind Jared Goff, this remains a top-10 passing attack that’s on the border of a top-five unit. The one thing they have been missing thus far is explosive plays. Through three games, the Lions have just nine passes of 20 yards or more, ranking 14th in the league. In each of the last four seasons, they’ve finished top-five in that statistical category. But teams are playing deep-shells against them and Detroit hasn’t found a way to pierce that coverage. Goff has just three passing attempts with 20 or more air yards (one completion), which is tied with Sam Darnold for the least in the NFL. The good news is that pass protection has been stellar so far for Detroit. Goff has faced a pressure rate of 32.2% (seventh lowest), has a sack rate of 6.0% (15th), while the offense line ranks second in pass-block win rate (60%), but 20th in PFF pass blocking grade. It’s hard to get a firm grasp on the Panthers’ pass defense. In Week 1, the Bears’ offense was just all over them, but they held their next two opponents relatively in check—although neither are the most explosive passing attacks in football. Through three weeks, the stats are inconclusive: Sixth in passer rating allowed (79.0) Sixth in yards per attempt (6.1) 11th in dropback EPA (0.004) 18th in success rate (46.8%) The first two data points are promising, but the last two may fall closer to reality given that the Panthers have faced two mediocre-at-best passing offenses—and have mostly seen the damage done on the ground . The main talking point about the Panthers’ passing defense has been the loss of their two starting cornerbacks this week. Both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn were placed on IR this week, leaving Will Lee and Akayleb Evans to step in. Admittedly, both players have flashed at time and won’t be pushovers, but they still represent significant downgrades. Carolina’s pass rush is better on paper than in practice thus far. Free agent defensive end addition Jaelan Phillips (12 pressures, 2.0 sacks) is an outstanding player, as is veteran defensive tackle Derrick Brown (six pressures), yet the overall stats for Carolina’s pass rush are underwhelming. They’re just 21st in pressure rate (24.2%), 19th in sack rate (6.0%), and 23rd in time to pressure (2.70 sec.). Player to watch: Amon-Ra St. Brown. The Panthers tend to lean heavy on zone and deep coverage—again trying to take away the explosives. So I expect St. Brown to eat over the middle, especially against less-experienced cornerbacks. Advantage: Lions +1.5. The only way I see the Lions losing this matchup is if the Panthers’ pass rush lives up to its billing finally. Carolina does like to send the extra heat, but Detroit proved they could handle it last week with Goff playing nearly perfect football against the blitz. I’m not sure how the Panthers’ reserve secondary will hold up against the Lions receivers, but it certainly seems like a favorable matchup. Lions run offense (2nd) vs. Panthers run defense (23rd) With the sample sizes so small, I am trying to pull back my optimism of the Lions’ rushing attack, but the early signs are very promising. I want to completely throw out Week 2, because of the injuries the Lions were dealing with on the offensive line, but that’s not completely fair. Still, even with that stinker of a game—in which the Lions also had to abandon the run—the Lions rushing efficiency metrics are optimistic. They rank: Ninth in yards per carry (4.4) 15th in rush EPA (-0.082) Fifth in rush success rate (48.1%) The only reason for Detroit’s low ranking in EPA is the lack of truly explosive plays. While the Lions have 11 rushes of 10+ yards (t-sixth most), they only have a single run over 20 yards to help skew the data this year. But the offensive line stats are stellar in the run game. Detroit ranks fifth in PFF run blocking grade (70.6), fifth in adjusted line yards, and fourth in rushing yards before contact per rush (2.06). This week, you’ve likely heard how bad the Panthers’ run defense is, and to an extent, that is true. However, it’s likely better than you think it is. Their season ranks are: 32nd in yards per carry allowed (5.7) 18th in rush EPA (-0.090) Ninth in success rate (35.6%) Those last two data points required some extra research, and I discovered the following. For one, the Panthers have been disproportionately impacted by quarterback runs through three games. Of their 580 rushing yards allowed, 25% of that yardage was damage done by mobile quarterbacks. That won’t be an issue this week . They’ve also given up a ton of big rushing plays—allowing five (most) rushes of 20+ yards. In between those splash plays, the Panthers have actually been okay. Not good, but okay. But one thing they haven’t done well is create negative plays: Carolina sports the second-lowest “stuffed rate” (rushes of 0 yards or less) in football with 8.9%. Player to watch: Devin Lloyd. Expected to be back after missing a game, Lloyd is the quarterback of the Panthers’ defense. Entering his fifth year and first with the Panthers, Lloyd brings a reputation of being a great all-around linebacker but specifically a stout run defender. He ranked 11th in PFF run defense grade in 2025 (85.2) and ninth in 2024 (84.2). Advantage: Lions +1.5. This could—and should—be the week the Lions break out a long run. And while I expect the Panthers run defense to be stouter than the numbers suggest, Detroit also has one of the best rushing attacks in football right now, and I don’t think the Panthers are equipped to stop them for four quarters. Panthers pass offense (15th) vs. Lions pass defense (26th) Okay, now the bad news. Bryce Young appears to be taking Year 4 by the horns, and is off to a very strong start. Thus far, the Panthers passing attack ranks: 16th in passer rating (95.6%) Eighth in yards per attempt (7.7) 14th in dropback EPA (0.130) 23rd in success rate (44.2%) Okay, so it’s not the most efficient passing attack in football despite ranking first in passing yards per game. The fact of the matter is this is a passing offense that is probably below average on a play-to-play basis, but is capable of an explosive play at any moment. This is highlighted by the fact that Carolina ranks just 28th in completion percentage (59.0), but has produced more 20+ yard passing plays (13) than anyone through three games. Pass protection has been a pretty big issue, with the Panthers allowing a league-high 43.6% pressure rate and seeing that pressure arrive at 2.52 seconds (fifth fastest). They rank 25th in pass block win…

title: Lions vs. Panthers preview: 3 key matchups
summary: It’s “Sunday Night Football” and the Detroit Lions have an opportunity to string together back-to-back wins when go on the road to take on the Carolina Panthers. Readers here at Pride of Detroit are spoiled. Truly. Before even getting to this key matchups article, coverage throughout the week have previewed this upcoming game from many […]
full_text: It’s “Sunday Night Football” and the Detroit Lions have an opportunity to string together back-to-back wins when go on the road to take on the Carolina Panthers. Readers here at Pride of Detroit are spoiled. Truly. Before even getting to this key matchups article, coverage throughout the week have previewed this upcoming game from many different perspectives. From Meko Scott and Morgan Cannon’s “Before the Roar” podcast, Erik Schlitt’s scheme breakdown , Ryan Matthews’ 5 Q’s , and much more from the rest of the staff and even beyond with Pride of Detroit Direct . All of that to say, as I begin finding my own space here I hope to provide thoughts and insights with these weekly key matchup previews that meet that standard set and go beyond the surface level. Digging deeper into not only what the matchups mean for each individual player, but for the team as a whole. Not only what the matchups may dictate for each particular game, but with future in mind as well. Every week I could write about which team is going to run the ball well and which is going to stop the run. I could write about the one-on-one wide receiver and cornerback matchup du jour every week. Rinse and repeat. I’d rather not. And I’d bet you’d rather something more than that as well. Time to dig in. Ennis Rakestraw Jr. vs. Ennis Rakestraw Jr. Lions cornerback Ennis Rakestraw Jr. showed flashes in his first action on the season against the Jets. His performance is by far the most meaningful development of any individual player through three games. If you’re reading this, I do not need to give you the numbers to prove the struggle of the Lions cornerbacks not only this season, but throughout the entirety of Dan Campbell’s tenure. I do not need to remind you about the multiple starters that necessitated a release due to off-field incidents. I do not need to remind you about the potential trade acquisition of Joey Porter Jr. that Brad Holmes did not make. What I may need to remind you about is that while Rakestraw is in this third year, he is just 24 years old. He was highly-touted, and often mocked to the Lions as a first-round pick in 2024 pre-draft coverage. He finished as the 32nd-best player on Daniel Jeremiah’s final big board. “About Ennis Rakestraw, has never been about his kind of what he could do and his skill set and what we were seeing on the field,” explained Kelvin Sheppard. “It had nothing to do with any of that. It was always about his availability with Ennis.” I could make this a matchup between Rakestraw and wide receivers Tetairoa McMillan or Jalen Coker, but I do not believe either player is Rakestraw’s biggest obstacle for successful in primetime. “I learned that I can play in this league,” Rakestraw said after his 2026 debut last week . “I finally got to play in a game, and I knew what kind of challenge it was going to be backside with No. 5, he’s paid a lot of money. Just had to step up to it.” If Rakestraw can continue his upward trajectory into Sunday night and begin to establish himself as a starting cornerback, the perception of and outlook for the defense will shift dramatically. But it’s up to him. Ennis vs. Ennis. “Just like I told [Ennis] Tuesday when he was in here. I said, ‘How much you play is up to you,’” Sheppard said. “We saw a very small sample size. Now lets see what that looks like on a larger scale and we’ll just take it from there.” Lions pass rush vs. Bryce Young The next key matchup of the contest I wanted to specifically highlight the pass rush as it relates to quarterback Bryce Young, not the Panther’s offensive line. There are a few reasons for this. First, the Panther’s offensive line is banged up with starting tackle Ikem Ekwonu on reserve/PUP, guard Damien Lewis not practicing with an elbow, and rookie first-round pick Monroe Freeling limited in practice in concussion protocol. With that being the case, I fully expect the Lions pass rush to have an advantage against the offensive line. At the bare minimum, Aidan Hutchinson and Alim McNeill should be to win their individual matchups relatively consistently. Per NFL Pro, Bryce Young currently faces the second-highest pressure rate among qualifying quarterbacks at 43.5% with the fifth-quickest average time to pressure of 2.56 seconds. On the other side of the equation, the Lions’ defensive pass rush is in the top-10 in pressure rate at 39% with the second-quickest average time to pressure of 2.46 seconds. The question is not whether the pass rush will create pressure quickly, but whether Young handles the pressure well and whether his ability to extend plays will result in explosive results. While under pressure, Young’s completion percentage sits at 49%, boosted by a 5.01% completion percentage over expected. Interestingly, under pressure his air yards per attempt is 14.3 while just 7.8 when not pressured. This feels like a make-or-break opportunity for the Lions, who are in the top five in explosive passing plays allowed this season. But with this tenancy evidenced in the metrics, there is an opportunity for Sheppard and Lions defenders to be cognizant of and to appropriately scheme against Young’s disparate pattern of throwing the ball further down field when feeling the heat. Jameson Williams vs. Ejiro Evero If you ran to the Panthers roster see if Ejiro Evero was one of the backup cornerbacks being thrust into a starting role due to the injuries of both starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson put them on IR , you probably aren’t alone. Ejiro Evero is one of the better defensive coordinators in the NFL, leading the Panthers defense since the 2023 season. The key matchup here is about how Evero decides to scheme against the Lions’ most feared offensive weapon. Not Jahmyr Gibbs. Not Amon-Ra St. Brown. Over the first three weeks of the season, the box score would tell you that Jameson Williams has been relatively absent from the Lions offense compared to expectations. But a deeper analysis shows just how much Williams has an effective on the game and how he implants fear deep within the soul of opposing defensive coordinators. “I was talking to [Jared Goff] about Wednesday out on the practice field,” said Sheppard. “Because Saint and Jamo were like, ’why are all of these defenses going to these 2-high? Scary. They’re scary.‘ I said, ‘Yeah, I’d be scared of ya’ll two as well.’ But the big thing its a consensus around the league if you look at it, most touchdown drives, there is an explosive pass play on the drive. It’s a real thing, guys.” The Panther’s run a significant amount of zone coverage defensively (85.2%), with the vast majority of that being cover-3 zone at 48.7%. Defensive coverage rates through Week 3 Via @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/m6XO0Z3Cbs — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) September 29, 2026 The question is going to be how the Panthers intend to handle Williams’ speed as he stretches the deep center of the field vertically, stressing free safety Nick Scott. Expect offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to test this matchup early to get as much information as possible as to the Panthers defense. Critically, defenses have remained committed to their deep shell-coverage against Williams. But eventually the dam will break. Enough Gibbs and St. Brown gut punches play-by-play and drive-over-drive while still resulting in a consistently cool 31 points of offensive production will force someone to flip the switch. When that game comes, watch out. Will it be you, Ejiro Evero? Three key matchups. Three opportunities.
author: Anthony Balaj

title: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Panthers in Week 4
summary: The Detroit Lions (2-1) and Carolina Panthers (1-2) will close out the Sunday slate of NFL games in Week 4, when the two battle it out on “Sunday Night Football.” “Going out to their place, ‘Sunday Night Football,’ Charlotte, North Carolina,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of this upcoming matchup. “It’ll be loud. It’s going […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 08: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions points at the line of scrimmage against the Carolina Panthers at Ford Field on October 08, 2023 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (2-1) and Carolina Panthers (1-2) will close out the Sunday slate of NFL games in Week 4, when the two battle it out on “Sunday Night Football.” “Going out to their place, ‘Sunday Night Football,’ Charlotte, North Carolina,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of this upcoming matchup. “It’ll be loud. It’s going to be one of those environments that we’ve got to be able to have poise under those circumstances. They’re coming off of a loss, and so they’re going to want to make that right. At home, big game for them. So, we’ll get their best shot […] This will be a good test. We’re looking forward to it.” Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Panthers in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1800 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 3.5-point favorites in Week 4 . Panthers base schemes For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 4 preview: Breaking down the Panthers’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Jared Goff beats Panthers blitz, thrives by taking what’s given Lions quarterback Jared Goff has been sensational through the first three weeks of the season, sporting the third-highest passer rating in the NFL at 116.1 and producing a 0.22 EPA per dropback, seventh-best. He’s been efficient against zone coverage (0.17 EPA, 13th), man coverage (0.54 EPS, 8th), in the red zone (0.55 EPA, 8th), and against the blitz (0.29 EPA, 8th). The Panthers run a bend-don’t-break version of Vic Fangio’s defensive scheme (see our weekly scheme breakdown for more details ). Their typical approach to defense is to cede short yardage plays to prevent explosives, force offenses to drive the length of the field on double-digit drives, and bank on offenses making a critical mistake before they reach the end zone. Despite the passive approach, the Panthers have surprisingly altered their approach this season by increasing their blitz rate: 44.4% overall (4th highest) and 37.6% on passing plays (7th highest), per NFL Pro. So, why would a defensive scheme known for its willingness to cede yards in small increments blitz so much? As Jeremy Reisman pointed out in his observations from the Panthers-Browns game , the Panthers simply aren’t generating enough pressure with just four rushers: No blitz: 33.3% pressure rate (10th), 2.93 seconds to pressure (22nd) Blitzing: 55.6% pressure rate (fourth highest), 2.76 seconds to pressure (29th) While the Panthers have seen production in this new approach, they may not have the same success against the Lions and Jared Goff. This season, Goff is completing 75.8% of his passing attempts against the blitz (5th best in the NFL) for 8.0 yards per attempt (10th) and four touchdowns. Last week he was flawless against the blitz; the Jets blitzed the Lions on 44% of plays, and Goff responded by completing all 14 of his passing attempts for 148 yards and a touchdown. If Goff can keep beating the blitz, the Lions’ skill players will have huge opportunities to eat after the catch (note: the Panthers have given up 286 YAC through three games, sixth most in the NFL). If the Panthers move away from the blitz and the Lions offensive line can keep him clean against just four rushers, look for Goff to adjust again and simply take what the defense gives him. Goff’s accuracy and risk-averse passes—along with the Lions skill players’ ability to create YAC—should allow Detroit to sustain drives and put up points. Prediction 2: Jahmyr Gibbs breaks 100 yards rushing… again With the Panthers looking to take away explosives, expect the Lions to try and take advantage of base and light boxes by feeding Jahmyr Gibbs. The Lions have leaned on Gibbs through three games (he’s accounted for 51% of the Lions’ offensive touches this season, per NFL Pro), and he’s delivered, producing a 57.8% success rate, the highest in the NFL. On paper, the Panthers’ run defense looks atrocious. They’re allowing 193.3 rush yards per game (last in the NFL), 5.7 rush yards per game (last), 13 rushes of 10 or more yards (29th), a minimal 8.9% stuffed rate (31st), and 3.85 yards after contact (32nd), landing them at 23rd in DVOA run defense rankings. Now, some of those numbers are skewed by a disastrous Week 1, but they still haven’t kept a team under 123 rush yards. Let’s look at how they did in each of their first three weeks: Week 1 vs. Bears (DVOA rushing: 9): 291 rush yards allowed, 7.5 yards per carry Week 2 vs. Falcons (DVOA rushing: 6): 123 allowed, 4.6 YPC Week 3 vs. Browns (DVOA rushing: 31): 132 allowed, 4.4 YPC While the Panthers certainly settled down since their game with the Bears, the Lions have an equally explosive offense and currently hold the No. 2 DVOA rushing attack, averaging 120 yards per game (9th), 4.4 yards per carry (9th), 11 rushes over 10 yards (7th), a rushing success rate of 48.2% (6th), per NFL Pro. In addition to Gibbs’ explosive ability, the Lions’ offensive line has also been getting consistent push in the run game. Despite not having Blake Miller and Christian Mahogany in Week 2, the Lions still average 2.06 yards before contact in the run game, the fourth-best mark in the NFL. Prediction 3: Lions take away Panthers’ rushing attack The Lions will always prioritize stopping the run, but like the Panthers, their numbers look worse than what the defense can actually do because one game skews a small sample size. Let’s take a look at how they did through the first three weeks of the season: Week 1 vs. Saints (DVOA rushing: 18): 91 rush yards allowed, 3.6 yards per carry, -0.03 EPA per rush Week 2 vs. Bills (DVOA rushing: 1): 203 allowed, 5.6 YPC, +0.37 EPA per rush Week 3 vs. Jets (DVOA rushing: 20): 58 allowed, 3.1 YPC, -0.23 EPA per rush Essentially, the Lions did their job against the bottom half of the league in rushing offenses, but struggled mightily against the Bills’ No. 1 DVOA rushing attack. While it’s still early in the season, the Panthers’ rushing attack certainly looks closer to being in the same bucket as the Saints and Jets than the Bills, and the statistics back that up: Panthers (DVOA rushing: 21st): 97 yards per game, 4.3 yards per carry, -0.11 EPA per rush With the defensive changes the Lions implemented against the Jets, several encouraging signs suggest the run defense is trending up. When defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard was asked what he thought his defense did well against the Jets, he pointed to their run defense. “Guys doing their job in the run game, just owning (their) gap. It starts with the front, being physical, changing the line of scrimmage. We want to play on their side of the line, […] We fire off, we get downhill on the second level, and we try to make things happen on their side of the line on our terms. And I think our guys have done that. “They’ve done it pretty well in two out of three games, and we all know what transpired at the Buffalo game. I want to give props to some of those players that had errors in the Buffalo game and the run game. The emphasis they took and the onus they took on to go out and make sure they weren’t a repeat offender.” Prediction 4: Lions disrupt Bryce Young with 4-man pressure Through the first two weeks of the season, we saw the Lions defense utilize the blitz to create pressure. Against the Saints, the Lions blitzed nearly 35% of snaps, then bumped that up to 55% against the Bills. The problem was that the Lions generated a pressure rate of only 43.4%, just slightly above the league average (43%), and were gashed in the secondary after sacrificing a player in coverage. After the Lions’ Week 3…

title: Packers film room: What went wrong on the Falcons 55-yard run
summary: Bijan Robinson’s 55-yarder against the Green Bay Packers in week three was the play that turned the game. It came on first down after a roughing the passer penalty on edge rusher Brenton Cox on third down that would have forced the Falcons to punt and given the Packers another chance to add to their […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - SEPTEMBER 24: Bijan Robinson #7 of the Atlanta Falcons celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers during an NFL football game at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Bijan Robinson’s 55-yarder against the Green Bay Packers in week three was the play that turned the game. It came on first down after a roughing the passer penalty on edge rusher Brenton Cox on third down that would have forced the Falcons to punt and given the Packers another chance to add to their 7-0 lead. The Packers took a 7-0 lead when Christian Watson came uncovered on a play-action pass with 5:13 left in the first quarter. Penix had also thrown an interception on Atlanta’s opening drive, so the Falcons’ offense looked out of sync. The drive that included the run nearly stalled too. Atlanta started at its own 15 and picked up a first down on an 8-yard pass to Kyle Pitts and a 6-yard Robinson run, but Lukas Van Ness forced Penix into an intentional grounding penalty that left Atlanta facing third-and-11. That was a likely punt situation, and Green Bay’s defense was winning. Instead, Brenton Cox Jr. was called for unnecessary roughness, which gave the Falcons a first down. Atlanta capitalized right away. On the very next snap, Robinson broke a 55-yard run to the Green Bay 5. The timing mattered as much as the yardage. A defense that has just given away a first down on a penalty is often a step slow to reset, and Robinson turned that moment into a huge gain. Going from backed up at the 15 to first-and-goal at the 5 within a couple of plays was the biggest field-position swing of the first half. The play call from Atlanta was an outside zone run concept to the offense’s left side behind their tight end Charlie Woerner and Drake London in tight to the formation. The Packers countered the Falcons formation with a 5-2 front and two deep safeties behind it. Playing two deep safeties versus the run is risky but the Packers have been excellent defending the run from two high shells the last couple of seasons and Gannon specializes in it. In fact, the Packers had it bottled up really well initially. Edgerrin Cooper (No. 56) is the edge setter on this play as the defensive end backdoor slants inside. Cooper is the spill/force player responsible for spilling the ball back inside. Zaire Franklin (No. 44) is the back side leverage player who’s job it is to clean up any open gap and the run if it spills back inside. On the perimeter, Brandon Cisse (No. 2) is the front side leverage player and secondary force. As Cooper comes down, Woerner blocks him and pancakes him to the ground. Cooper plays the inside shoulder and leaves Cisse on an island if Robinson bounces outside. Sure enough he does as Franklin moves with Robinson’s movement and flashes color in the gaps. Cisse dives for the tackle and misses. The rookie did not have a great night. A tackle here would have went for a one or two yard gain. Poor gap responsibility ultimately doomed the defense on this play. Robinson later scored on a 3-yard run two plays later, tying the game at 7 with 1:32 left in the first quarter. From there, Atlanta took over. The Falcons scored 27 straight points, turning a 7-0 deficit into a 27-7 lead in the fourth quarter. The run was also the first sign of how the night would go on the ground. Robinson finished with 194 yards and two touchdowns on 29 carries, one yard short of his career high of 195 set against the Rams in 2025. Green Bay managed almost nothing running the ball by comparison. The Packers ran nine times for just 17 yards.
author: Rich Madrid

title: Remembering the Packers’ best performances against the Buccaneers
summary: The Green Bay Packers head to Tampa, Florida this weekend for a date with their old NFC Central opponents, the Buccaneers.  Setting aside our memories of the 2020 NFC Championship, there were plenty of great matchups between the Packers and Buccaneers over the years, and they produced quite a few high-end statistical performances. Here are […]
full_text: MILWAUKEE, WI - SEPTEMBER 12: Lynn Dickey #12 of the Green Bay Packers looks to pass against the Los Angeles Rams during an NFL football game September 12, 1982 at Milwaukee County Stadium in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Dickey played for the Packers from 1976-85. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers head to Tampa, Florida this weekend for a date with their old NFC Central opponents, the Buccaneers. Setting aside our memories of the 2020 NFC Championship, there were plenty of great matchups between the Packers and Buccaneers over the years, and they produced quite a few high-end statistical performances. Here are some of the best, with links throughout to some highlights that are just about guaranteed to give you a jolt of nostalgia. Most passing yards – 418 ( Lynn Dickey, 1980 ) Packers fans should have plenty of good memories of great passing days against the Buccaneers — five different Packers quarterbacks have broken the 300-yard mark against Tampa! But the greatest of them all isn’t Aaron Rodgers or Brett Favre or even Don Majkowski. It’s Lynn Dickey, who rolled up 418 yards in a game the Packers thoroughly dominated , but didn’t win. Despite outgaining the Buccaneers by more than 300 yards (569 to 262), two turnovers and three missed field goals prevented the Packers from coming out on top. Instead, the game ended in a 14-14 tie, which remains the only tie between these two teams in their relatively long history together. Most rushing yards – 169 ( Ahman Green, 2001 ) Ahman Green’s 169 yard day would be more impressive if he could have hung onto the ball. Really, turnovers were the entire theme of the Packers’ 2001 home matchup against their NFC Central opponents — the last time they’d play their division rivals at home before the Buccaneers headed off for the NFC South. Green’s fumble was one of three turnovers by the Packers that day and came smack in the middle of a seven-drive series of remarkable futility. After scoring a touchdown on their first drive of the game, the Packers’ next seven drives went like so: punt, interception, punt, fumble, missed field goal, interception, punt. Yet thanks in part to Green, who scored on a 63-yard scamper in the third quarter, the Packers’ still hung around long enough for one big play to turn the tide later. More on that in a bit. Most receiving yards – 169 ( Sterling Sharpe, 1989 ) In a funny historical coincidence, the Packers’ single-game receiving yardage high against the Buccaneers is the same as their single game rushing yardage high, and somewhat predictably, it belongs to Sterling Sharpe. Sharpe had 130 or more receiving yards against the Buccaneers four different times, but never put up a bigger yardage number than he did in an eight catch, 169 yard, two touchdown performance against the Buccaneers in 1989. Sharpe’s performance was the first of three times a Packers player would have 150 or more receiving yards against the Buccaneers, and the other two guys to do it pulled it off in the same game. In 1999 , both Bill Schroeder and Antonio Freeman surpassed 150 receiving yards ; Schroeder had seven catches for 158 yards, while Freeman had seven catches for just 152, but added two touchdowns, the second a 21-yard strike that gave the Packers the win. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden: your targets are set for Sunday. Most points – 24 ( Sterling Sharpe, 1993 ) Remember earlier when I mentioned Sterling Sharpe had four different games where he put up more than 130 receiving yards against the Buccaneers? Yeah, that 169-yard game was arguably not his best. In 1993, Sharpe caught 10 passes for 147 yards and scored four touchdowns — three of which came in the first half. The Packers cruised to a 37-14 win behind Sharpe’s massive day. Most sacks – 4.5 ( Bryce Paup, 1991 ) Big days aren’t limited to the offense, of course. En route to a 15-13 Packers’ win , Bryce Paup and the rest of the defense put Vinny Testaverde in hell, sacking him seven times, with Paup accounting for 4.5. One of Paup’s sacks came in the end zone, giving him the first (but not only) points of his NFL career. Most solo tackles – 10 (two players tied) Here’s a chance to think about two guys who probably haven’t crossed your mind in a while. The Packers’ high water mark for solo tackles against the Buccaneers is 10 and it’s happened twice. Jude Waddy did it first, taking down 10 players by himself in 1999. Tyrone Williams did it two years later, racking up 10 solo tackles in the same game where Ahman Green ran for 169 yards. Most interceptions – 2 (eight players tied) Eight different players have had two interceptions in a game against the Buccaneers, so we’ve got a bunch of different performances from which to choose if we’re looking for a highlight. How’s this one for you? LeRoy Butler intercepted two passes in the Packers’ 1996 season-opening win over the Buccaneers, setting the tone for their Super Bowl journey. Oh, and since I have a contractual obligation to mention tight ends whenever possible, Keith Jackson scored three touchdowns that day. Let’s see it again, Tucker Kraft! Honorable mention: Allen Rossum scores on a punt return to beat the Buccaneers I mentioned earlier there were some heroics that delivered the win for the Packers in the game where Ahman Green ran for 169 yards, and here they are. After the Packers’ defense forced a punt late in the fourth quarter, Allen Rossum ripped off a 55-yard punt return for a touchdown to give the Packers a 21-20 win over the Buccaneers in 2001. Was it a pretty game? Certainly not. But Rossum’s effort gave the Packers an exciting win over Tampa in their last meetings as divisional rivals, and that’s always going to be worth remembering.

title: Packers Injury Report: Green Bay rules out starting guards
summary: The Green Bay Packers have ruled out four players on their final injury report for Week 4, before taking on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers: starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), starting right guard Jacob Monk (quadricep), defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf/groin) and defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle). Surprisingly, the Packers can make up these losses, […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have ruled out four players on their final injury report for Week 4, before taking on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers: starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), starting right guard Jacob Monk (quadricep), defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf/groin) and defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle). Surprisingly, the Packers can make up these losses, at least in terms of numbers, with their active roster, as the team is already “oversigned” on both the offensive and defensive lines. With these four players ruled out, Green Bay only needs to make one more scratch to get their 53-man roster down to a 48-man game-day roster on Sunday. Banks’ injury replacement appears to be Laken Tomlinson, who received snaps at left guard in media-open portions of practice this week. Right guard is more complicated, as Donovan Jennings, Travis Glover and the recently signed Kevin Zeitler all got looks to prep them to play the position this week. LaFleur said that Zeitler will be the team’s season-long answer at right guard when he’s caught up on the offense, but there are still questions about whether or not Zeitler will be able to go immediately. Tomlinson, another signing this week for the Packers, is hitting the ground running a little quicker. One reason why that could be possible? There’s a lot of crossover between the systems he’s played in previously and Green Bay’s system. Tomlinson was in San Francisco with current Packers offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich (then the assistant offensive line coach), and was under offensive coordinators Mike LaFleur, head coach and play-caller Matt’s younger brother, and Nathaniel Hackett, a former LaFleur offensive coordinator. Beyond the players who are ruled out, starting linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (shoulder/concussion) and backup interior offensive lineman Jager Burton (groin) were listed as questionable today. Cooper was a limited participant on both Wednesday and Thursday, but was elevated to a full participant on Friday. Burton was a full participant on Wednesday but dropped down to a limited participant on Thursday and Friday. Even if Burton can’t go, the Packers’ shouldn’t need to bring up a practice squad offensive lineman, as they carry a league-leading 11 offensive lineman on their 53-man roster . For reference, most teams carry eight offensive linemen on the game-day roster, as the league has an exemption for the 48th man (really, the league’s game-day roster rules are for a 47-man roster and an exemption), if and only if that 48th man is an eighth offensive lineman. To make this real simple (assuming that Cooper can pass concussion protocol fully), the Packers’ five scratches this week are expected to be the four players they’ve already ruled out due to injury plus an offensive lineman (be it Burton or someone else). Currently, this is the roster count for Green Bay’s offensive linemen on the 53-man roster: Jordan Morgan (preferred left tackle) Laken Tomlinson (injury replacement left guard) Sean Rhyan (preferred center) Anthony Belton (injury replacement right tackle) Kevin Zeitler (right guard option) Donovan Jennings (right guard option) Travis Glover (right guard option) Jager Burton (questionable) John Williams (backup left tackle) Aaron Banks (OUT) Jacob Monk (OUT) The Buccaneers ruled out first-round rookie pass-rusher Rueben Bain Jr. with a groin/shoulder injury today, along with listing starting cornerback Jacob Parrish, who has missed two practices this week with a personal injury, as questionable for Sunday. #Packers injury report: G Aaron Banks, G Jacob Monk, DT Warren Brinson and DT Anthony Campbell are out. pic.twitter.com/eZ6Cb6WRPp — Tom Silverstein (@TomSilverstein) October 2, 2026

title: Packers film room: Brief notes on the defense’s coverage bust in week 3
summary: The Packers week three defense against Atlanta, at least versus the Falcons pass game, was defined by two plays. Drake London caught passes of 68 and 40 yards in the fourth quarter, catches that helped him finished with nine catches for a career-high 194 yards, The 68-yarder and the 40-yarder given up by the defense […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Drake London #5 of the Atlanta Falcons runs with the ball after a catch against Brandon Cisse #2 of the Green Bay Packers during the fourth quarter of the game at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers week three defense against Atlanta, at least versus the Falcons pass game, was defined by two plays. Drake London caught passes of 68 and 40 yards in the fourth quarter, catches that helped him finished with nine catches for a career-high 194 yards, The 68-yarder and the 40-yarder given up by the defense accounted for 108 of those yards and led directly to 10 of Atlanta’s points. Atlanta led 24-7 heading into the fourth quarter. The 4th quarter opened with Penix hitting London for 68 yards on third-and-2 from deep in their own territory. The down and distance is a high leverage down for the Falcons. On third-and-2, a defense has to respect the short game, including the run, the quick slant, and the flat, and Green Bay’s coverage lost London in the process. The defense is playing single high cover-3 to protect the short area and be in a position to defend the run. Brandon Cisse is the corner to the weak side aligned about seven yards off and to the outside of London who is in a stack alignment off the ball with the tight end. The Falcons have a 2×2 four verticals concept called and this is the ideal defensive coverage to run it against. Running four verticals against single high coverage can put the safety in a bind because the quarterback can manipulate the safety’s movement and move him away from a vertical matchup he wants. That’s what quarterback Michael Penix does here. Xavier McKinney, as the deep safety, bails to the deep third down the boundary hash but Penix’s eyes move him away from the boundary. Cisse inexplicably pushes to the flat as London gives him and out and up move and he doesn’t run with him initially. He only does once he realizes he has no help over the top. The result is a coverage bust and wide open throwing window for Penix. The drive didn’t finish with a touchdown. A holding penalty and Javon Bullard’s two-yard tackle for loss on Brian Robinson stalled it, and Nick Folk’s 31-yard field goal made it 27-7 with 10:57 left. Even so, adding points on that possession effectively ended the game with nearly 11 minutes to play. After this, Green Bay made a push to get back in it. Jordan Love hit Matthew Golden for a 15-yard touchdown on a slant, cutting the lead to 27-14 with 8:18 left. The Falcons responded with a drive to keep the Packers from building momentum. After Bijan Robinson picked up four yards on third-and-2, London caught a 40-yard pass that took the ball to the Packers’ 13. Later in the game, Penix hit London on a 40-yarder that was more about London beating tight coverage. It would’ve been a contested pass with cornerback Keisean Nixon but fell down in coverage as the ball arrived. Nixon was initially in position over the top inside of London and was locked up until the point London disengaged to track the ball well to the inside of his route. he fell down as the two disengaged from contact and Penix trusted his receiver’s size and hands. London jumped inside and caught the ball in mid air. Bijan Robinson finished the drive with a two-yard touchdown run, and a successful two-point conversion made it 35-14 with 3:33 left.

title: Packers DL Warren Brinson to miss a ‘significant amount of time’
summary: Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said in his pre-practice press conference on Friday that defensive lineman Warren Brinson will miss a “significant amount of time” after he slipped and injured himself during Wednesday’s practice. Brinson was seen working out with the defensive line group in the media-open portion of practice on Wednesday, but […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said in his pre-practice press conference on Friday that defensive lineman Warren Brinson will miss a “significant amount of time” after he slipped and injured himself during Wednesday’s practice. Brinson was seen working out with the defensive line group in the media-open portion of practice on Wednesday, but dropped out of action and spent time with the team’s medical staff. On Thursday, Brinson was a non-participant. Brinson hasn’t played in a game this season, due to the fact that he injured his calf in pre-game warmups going into the Packers’ Week 2 preseason matchup against the Denver Broncos. After Brinson’s recent injury, he was given the status of “calf/groin,” rather than just “calf,” so the assumption is that his new injury is to his groin. Green Bay generally uses five interior defensive linemen on their game-day roster for its 3-4 defense, and the team has seven players at the position on the 53-man roster, so they’re “oversigned” on the defensive line. Brinson’s injury doesn’t present an immediate need to backfill the position on the 53-man roster, which is currently full, but it does knock the team’s depth a bit. For what it’s worth, Karl Brooks (illness) was a non-participant on Wednesday but a limited participant on Thursday, a sign that he’s trending in a positive direction for being a game-day active, while Anthony Campbell (ankle) has missed back-to-back practices this week. As long as Brooks can go on Sunday, the Packers should have five interior defensive linemen in Brooks, Devonte Wyatt, Javon Hargrave, Jonathan Ford and rookie third-round pick Chris McClellan. If Brooks can’t suit up (along with Brinson and Campbell), there’s a chance that practice squadder David Blay Jr. — who was just signed this week — might have to be called up against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

title: Cheese Curds: Fans hoping Packers look a little different on Sunday
summary: The Green Bay Packers are going to look different on offense Sunday. At least that’s what I keep telling myself in the mirror every morning.  After three weeks of struggles punctuated by a hundred-year weather event at the offensive line position, the Packers have made an unprecedented series of changes. Green Bay added veteran guards […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Green Bay Packers fans look on during the second quarter of the game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are going to look different on offense Sunday. At least that’s what I keep telling myself in the mirror every morning. After three weeks of struggles punctuated by a hundred-year weather event at the offensive line position, the Packers have made an unprecedented series of changes. Green Bay added veteran guards Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton in a matter of days, with Tomlinson and Zeitler both potentially in line for starting roles against Tampa Bay (Zeitler may not start this week but was seen taking a mix of shadow reps and real ones in practice). The hope is that experience can stabilize an offensive line that has been overwhelmed by injuries and inconsistent play. Appearing this week on the UnPack Podcast , Justis Mosqueda noted that much of the problem has been twofold: two young guards who don’t understand the nuances of the blocking scheme and a center who is playing worse because he’s trying to compensate for the guards. The three veterans the Packers have brought in have combined for 434 career starts. If nothing else, they’ll understand what they’re supposed to be doing. That’s the idea anyway. And that could also give Matt LaFleur an opportunity to simplify the running game and finally establish some consistency on the ground. Enter: Kaleb Johnson. With Marshawn Lloyd proving he’s not up to the starting back task, Johnson is poised to see his workload increase. And with a beefed up offensive line keeping it simple and moving mass up front, Johnson seems like the logical choice to “take ball run forward.” Tampa Bay’s run defense can be tough, but Sunday could provide the first indication of whether Johnson is capable of handling something approaching a bell-cow workload. Though, all they really need is for him to be just productive enough to take some pressure off the line and Jordan Love. That alone could make the offense much more fun to watch on Sunday. But wait, there’s more. The Packers will also have to compensate for the loss of Jayden Reed, whose season-ending neck surgery removes a versatile weapon. LaFleur has indicated that Skyy Moore, Bo Melton and J. Michael Sturdivant will share the responsibility rather than any one player simply replacing Reed. Do three bonafide Guys equal one starting caliber wide receiver? We’ll see! Put it all together, and Sunday’s game could be about more than just the result. It could be the first signs of some open wounds beginning to heal. But, you know, in an entertaining way. full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 18: Houston Texans DE Derek Barnett (95) scoops up a fumble during game featuring the Houston Texans and the Dallas Cowboys on November 18, 2024 at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, TX. (Photo by John Rivera/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images How are we here again? Your Houston Texans are 0-3. The offense, full of weapons, is struggling to put more than 18 points per game on the board and suddenly, this is a must-win match up against the Oklahoma South Cowboys. Fanduel ‘s odds currently have the Texans down by 3 . Will Kaimi Fairbairn take that bet and kick H-Town to their first win of 2026? Hopefully it won’t come to that. However, the betting site’s first prop bet has the Texans opening drive ending in a field goal as a more likely outcome than a touchdown. Texans fan and BRB faithful Sarlegant pointed out a recent Seth Payne video the other day where former H-Town defender Payne unpacks some Texans truths. After listening to head coach Demeco Ryans discuss the coaching staff, play calling and some other nifty tidbits in the video,, there is hope for Battle Red Nation! If you’re unfamiliar with Seth Payne, despite his humorous self-deprecation, he holds a very unique place in local Texans coverage. As a former player, highly intelligent student of the game and passionate Texans fan, Payne has unique access and insights into the organization, coaching, schemes and on-field results. When he breaks things down, you’ll likely learn something new, and chuckle more than once along the way. Reason for hope : the offense gets Nico Collins and Ed Ingram back this week. Dallas pulled off a newsworthy trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers this week to secure cornerback Joey Porter Jr., who may start this weekend. Cowboy fans think that’s fantastic. Texans fans remember Collins facing Porter in the playoffs last season. Prediction One: Nico Collins scores on Joey Porter Jr. While Collins did not have a stellar outing in the Texans 30-6 blowout of the Steelers in last season’s wild card, Nico is a “put the team on your back and win” kind of player. Sitting on the sidelines, watching his teammates struggle to move the ball and score points has him chomping at the bit. With Tank Dell still out, Jayden Higgins on IR and the tight ends serving as o-linemen, Collins will get quarterback C.J. Stroud’s attention early and often. Expect him to step up. Prediction Two: Will Anderson Jr. has 3 sack game. Much has been said about the “players only” meeting led by Anderson Jr. last week. While not every player on the defense seemed to respond against the Indianapolis Colts, it’s very clear Anderson Jr. is on a mission to win a Super Bowl, even if he has to do it all by himself. Dak Prescott has been sacked 3 times so far in 2026, but he’s yet to face a defense like Houston’s. With the need to hold the ball a little longer, his desire to scramble will rise. Derek Stingley Jr. had 2 breakups and an interception the last time these teams met and Prescott will remember. And with that memory, he opens himself up to pressure from Danielle Hunter, Sheldon Rankins, Jadeveon Clowney and Anderson Jr. Reason for hope: Despite Ryans’ recent insistence that offensive coordinator Nick Caley will continue to call the plays, Ryans low-key admits things are not working as they should. How does this play out heading into this weekend’s game? Hopefully other voices (Stroud, QB coach Jerry Shuplinski, Ryans) will speak into the play calling. This offense has the talent to perform, just not the way Caley seems to think they should. On paper the Cowboys seem like the better team so far in 2026. But they’ve not stood toe-to-toe with a team like Josh Allen’s Buffalo Bills. Houston has, and nearly won. Prediction Three: Dallas Cowboys 19 Houston Texans 31 The Texans are due for a breakout game. H-town football fanship is perpetually sailing through rough seas, but for every trough between waves, there’s a crest to keep us all hoping for more. The offense seems to suddenly click, the defense contributes a touchdown, and Dare Ogunbowale will reignite the special teams. title: Five Good Texans Questions with Blogging the Boys
summary: Like the Olympics, the battle with the interstate rivals comes every four years. It is never a disappointment because someone in the state is getting bragging rights. Fortunately, we have some consistency here at five questions and so I get to catch up with David Halprin of Blogging the Boys yet again. It was good […]
full_text: Like the Olympics, the battle with the interstate rivals comes every four years. It is never a disappointment because someone in the state is getting bragging rights. Fortunately, we have some consistency here at five questions and so I get to catch up with David Halprin of Blogging the Boys yet again. It was good catching up with him again. Like the Texans, the Cowboys suffered a disappointing loss late and that is where our conversation hegan. Battle Red Blog: The Cowboys are obviously coming off a tough loss overseas to the Ravens. Are you concerned about a hangover? David Haprin: At this point, I’m concerned about everything Dallas Cowboys. Well, maybe not their ability to throw the ball on offense, but outside of that, nothing has been really solid in Dallas. In the Ravens game, the biggest cause of the loss was HC Brian Schottenheimer, something he has admitted himself. His play-calling in certain situations was abysmal and he knows it. In a weird way, if you look at a lot of things that happened in that game, the Cowboys played pretty well, especially considering the amount of injuries they have on defense. They got their run game going, their defense had some splash plays that kept them in the game, but mistakes on the field, and especially along the sideline, really cost them. They were in position to beat the Ravens, and beat them pretty handily. But they threw it all away. Will there be a hangover from that? Maybe, one never knows with this team. BRB: The Cowboys offense has always been able to move the ball and score points. Are there any new wrinkles that fans from outside of Cowboys Nation might not be expecting? DH: I wouldn’t say much has changed since that part of the team went virtually untouched from last season. From the coaches, to the starters, even to some of the backups, it is a unit with a high continuity level. They will do what they do. They love to run Javonte Williams between the tackles. They will give a lot of eye candy pre-snap, and they use movement blocking from their offensive line in the run game in diverse ways, but essentially what they want is Williams chewing up yards between the tackles. That allows them the freedom to use their passing game, which is the star of the show in Dallas. Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens are the best thing Dallas has going for them. Outside of his playoff issues, Prescott is a stats machine. Lamb and Pickens can be used all over the field. Pickens is thought of as a deep ball, contested-catch specialist, but the Cowboys will throw a short slant to him also. Lamb can be used everywhere, even on screens. Backing them up are TE Jake Ferguson and WR3 Ryan Flournoy. As long as their offensive line holds up, they will score points. BRB: Obviously the Cowboys defense has been more shaky. What is the key for them getting back on track? DH: I mean, at this point, we are just hoping for performances where they hold the team in the game so the offense can win it. That usually means making a few splash plays in a game to create a turnover, a fourth-down stop, or something that gives the offense the ball in decent position. They don’t have a good pass rush, that is one of their problems. They are okay creating pressure, but they don’t get sacks. Mobile QBs also really hurt them. They are also not great against the run, although they did a decent job of keeping Derrick Henry in check last Sunday. Their biggest problem right now is the injuries in the secondary. The Cowboys defense has suffered an inordinate amount of injuries recently, with a large cluster in the secondary. We almost ran out of bodies back there against the Ravens. Rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham and rookie safety Caleb Downs have been the best players on that side of the ball. The Cowboys need some of their veterans, like Quinnen Williams, Rashan Gary and a few others to start playing up to their abilities to get close to back on track. BRB: Are there any key injuries that could have a significant impact on the game on Sunday? DH: Short answer – absolutely. Long answer – on offense, we are still without our best lineman in G Tyler Smith, but sub T.J. Bass has been great. On defense: Starting CB Cobie Durant has been out, and will likely miss this week, too. Starting LB DeMarvion Overshown has been out but it is possible he suits up this week. Starting S Malik Hooker has been out but he could also be back this week. Starting S Jalen Thompson was hurt in the Ravens game and is likely going to IR. Top backup CB Shavon Revel was hurt in the Ravens game and his status is unknown. Top backup S P.J. Locke has been put on IR. Backup DT Jonathan Bullard might go to IR. BRB: How do you see the game going on Sunday? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? DH: Honestly, I am so unsure this week. The Cowboys are Jekyll and Hyde, sometimes in the same game. We just never know how they will play. But it is early in the season and I am still an optimist, so I am going to take the Cowboys for the win, but it is going to be a close one. The Cowboys offense will move the ball, even against really good defenses they can usually generate some points, but their defense can make the most mediocre of offenses look all-world. In the end, I’m betting, speaking of prop bets, on the trio of Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. They will lead Dallas to a squeaker of a win. We wanted to thank David again for taking the time to answer our questions and for being so easy to work with again after four long seasons. We want to wish David and the Cowboys the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As per usual, we hope that luck begins on Monday morning.
