full_text: The Miami Dolphins fell to the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday, dropping to 0-3 as they continue navigating a significant roster rebuild. While wins and losses matter, much of the focus in 2026 remains on the development of Miami’s young talent. That is especially true along the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea are important pieces of the team’s future. How are they performing this season? Each week, we take a closer look at the guards and what is being said about their most recent performance. Kadyn Proctor Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 1 71.2 79.0 63.4 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 2 62.0 72.4 39.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 57.5 51.1 71.3 Jonah Savaiinaea Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 0 47.6 50.9 38.2 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 0 65.9 68.5 46.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 56.6 58.4 47.5 What We Learned The grades paint a mixed picture of Miami’s performance against Kansas City, but there were still encouraging signs from the Dolphins’ young guards. For the first time this season, Miami did not allow a sack, and on Ollie Gordon’s touchdown run , Kadyn Proctor executed an impressive pull to the left, sealing off Chiefs safety Jaden Hicks before helping escort (forcefully) Gordon into the end zone. While that play was a highlight, there is still room for growth in pass protection. Proctor and Jonah Savaiinaea were each charged with two pressures, while the offensive line surrendered nine hurries overall. Even so, Proctor showed improvement as a pass protector, earning a 71.3 pass-blocking grade from PFF after posting a 39.1 mark the previous week. The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins .

(Photo by Nick Wosika/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins visit the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday and will see plenty of familiar faces on the opposing sidelines. Vikings practice squad linebacker Kyle Van Noy played in Miami in 2020 while Minnesota’s coaching staff includes defensive backs coach Gerald Alexander, who played safety for the Dolphins in 2011 and was Miami’s defensive backs coach in 2020 and 2021; defensive assistant Charlie Frye was Miami’s quarterbacks coach in 2021; passing game coordinator Josh McCown was a training camp quarterback in 2008; assistant head coach Frank Smith was Miami’s offensive coordinator from 2022 through 2025; and Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell was a training camp quarterback for the Dolphins in 2011. Of course, Minnesota defensive coordinator Brian Flores was the head coach for the Dolphins from 2019 through 2021. And perhaps the most recognizable person on the field for Dolphins fans, with his hair flowing out from under his helmet, will be linebacker Andrew Van Ginkel. AVG played for the Dolphins from 2019 through 2023, appearing in 73 games, including 42 starts, recording 2019 tackles, 17 sacks, two interceptions, seven passes defensed, three forced fumbles, three fumble recoveries, and two touchdowns. A 2019 fifth-round pick for Miami out of Wisconsin, Van Ginkel signed as a free agent with the Vikings in 2024, taking a fan favorite out of the Miami defense and reuniting him with Flores. Miami Dolphins on SI writer Alain Poupart took a look at the one who got away as Miami prepares to face the Vikings: Former Miami Dolphins safety Jevon Holland is off to a great start in his second season with the New York Giants and he was recognized Thursday as the NFC Defensive Player of the Month. He’s not, however, somebody the Dolphins should regret not having retained as a free agent two offseasons ago. Andrew Van Ginkel, who the Dolphins will face for the first time since he left when they take on the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, is an entirely different story… It was one thing to debate whether the Dolphins should have done whatever it took to keep former draft picks like Christian Wilkins, Robert Hunt and/or Holland instead of having them leave as free agents instead of spending big money on outsiders like Tyreek Hill and Jalen Ramsey, but the conversation should have been much simpler with Van Ginkel. At some point, he’s going to have to start doing something, you would think, and this week seems like as good a week as any. Vikings to have 7+ kicking points (-200) Will Reichard is the best kicker in the National Football League, bar none. We know that. Obviously, the Vikings should be scoring touchdowns on Sunday, as the Dolphins’ red zone defense is terrible, but given that Minnesota’s offense has been nothing to write home about so far this season, I’m guessing we’ll see #16 trot out onto the field a couple of times on Sunday afternoon, and when he does, he’s going to do what Will Reichard always does. Those are my picks for the best player prop bets for the Vikings this week when they face off with the Dolphins at U.S. Bank Stadium. Are there any that you’ve got your eye on?

title: Current State of Affairs for the Minnesota Vikings
summary: I don’t know if I have ever been less inspired by a 3-0 start than I have been this NFL season. I love the Vikings, and want nothing more than for this team to succeed. The narrative of our incredible, potentially historic defense and our deflated, stagnant offense has pretty much run its course already. […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Will Reichard #16 of the Minnesota Vikings and Brett Thorson #19 celebrate after a field goal against the Chicago Bears during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images I don’t know if I have ever been less inspired by a 3-0 start than I have been this NFL season. I love the Vikings, and want nothing more than for this team to succeed. The narrative of our incredible, potentially historic defense and our deflated, stagnant offense has pretty much run its course already. Everyone and their mama knows that this formula for winning is not sustainable. When you are three games in and your kicker has accounted for more points than your starting quarterback, that’s a problem in my eyes. Thank goodness we have future Hall of Famer Will Reichard. Funny enough, the pick we received from the Jets, in our trade to move up one spot to draft J.J. McCarthy, was Will the Thrill. Herein Lies the Power Speaking of trading J.J. McCarthy, I think we saw a shift in power within the Minnesota Vikings organization. That shift went from Kevin O’Connell being a major contributor to offensive draft selections and free agent signings to Nolan Teasley asserting his authority as the personnel decision-maker. I really don’t mind this, because I think KO’s strengths lie in his coaching ability. I can’t help but get the feeling that Kevin O’Connell is on the hot seat more than any other 3-0 head coach has been on the hot seat. I know Brian Flores is on this staff, but there has not been an instance in NFL history, from what I’ve been able to find, of a coach with a strong winning record being fired or demoted mid-season. As strong as Teasley’s grasp on this franchise might be, it’s not strong enough to “elevate” Brian Flores to head coach (much to the chagrin of some Daily Norseman Faithful). Is KOC’s Future in Jeopardy? I’ve had this take before, but I don’t think I have shared it here, and if I have, it’s been a while. The take is this: Kevin O’Connell will not be the head coach of the Minnesota Vikings in 2027 if he fails to WIN a playoff game this season. I think that is where the standard lies, and there are historical circumstances of winning coaches being fired due to postseason ineffectiveness. Most notable was Marty Schottenheimer in 2006, who was fired after a 14-2 season with MVP LaDainian Tomlinson, which culminated in a divisional-round collapse against the New England Patriots. That being said, I think O’Connell is a good head coach. His job entails so much more than calling plays and game planning for the offense. Maybe he has too much on his plate ,and it’s time for him to lean on his offensive coordinator, Wes Phillips, a little bit more. The Recipe for Success Yes, watching our offense, at times, makes me want to drink water from a stagnant pond and line my stomach and intestines with bacteria and amoebas, just so I can be so debilitated that I can’t even look at a TV screen. Every time Aaron Jones touches the ball, I think about how I get sore (as a 36-year-old man) after sleeping on my neck funny. This dude is getting popped, smacked, and crushed multiple times a game. The commitment to the run game is refreshing. We have been running more on this 8-game winning streak dating back to last season, but why is that? Is it because the run game is so effective that we are grinding teams down and asserting our dominance on offense? No, however, the running game is effectively eating up the clock in hopes that we can maybe score 13 points and keep the other team’s offense off the field for as long as possible. The longer we hold the ball on offense, the stronger the defense becomes. The passing game isn’t in shambles, per se, but there is massive room for improvement. Kevin O’Connell mentioned in a press conference that it seemed as though the Buccaneers had a very deliberate plan to swat down Murray’s passes. I’ve seen Cardinals fans commenting on social media posts about how we are learning about Kyler what they’ve known for years. Yes, he is incredibly short in stature for an NFL quarterback, and yes, that means he can’t always see what’s happening down the field. We are not seeing the scrambling generator of yards that I think NFL fans are used to seeing with Kyler Murray. There is definitely an emphasis on taking care of the football and trusting the processes and play calls. I think Kyler did a fine job protecting the football against Tampa Bay, and his interception was mainly caused by Blake Brandel’s questionable decision to bat the ball up in the air to make the interception that much easier for the defensive lineman. Halfway to Competent Quarterback Play On a promising note, we did see some success from Kyler Murray on deep balls that we were desperately missing last season. Although this is promising, we also saw Murray struggle on shorter passes. According to NFL Next Gen Stats: Murray completed three of four passes over 20 air yards in that half for 93 yards, the most deep completions by a Vikings quarterback in a first half since Sam Bradford in 2016. Murray completed just 12 of 20 passes under 20 air yards for 75 yards and an interception. This makes me hopeful that we will start to see things click and maybe our offense can score more touchdowns. When this team was struggling last season, it was because we either A. couldn’t protect the quarterback or B. our quarterback was throwing the ball to the other team on a regular basis. The Max Brosmer start versus the Seattle Seahawks will always haunt my memory. Murray has only played one full game in this system. Even the great Sam Darnold took a couple of games to get going in his first and only season with this team. It wasn’t until that 49ers game with that huge pass to Justin Jefferson that the offense really started clicking. There are Still 14 Games to Play At the end of the day, the Minnesota Vikings are winning football games in 2026. They are currently the first seed in the NFC if the playoffs started today. They have a trap game test on Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. If they’re able to come out with a convincing win, I will be able to breathe a little easier. I guess we will see. Until Next Skol.

title: Week 4 Preview: A Passing Interest
summary: The Minnesota Vikings return home to U.S. Bank Stadium on Sunday to face a 0-3 Miami Dolphins team looking ahead to the 2027 NFL Draft. Their best offensive player, De’Von Achane, is officially out for the year with a torn ACL suffered last week. The Dolphins are tied for the league low with 36 points […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 16: Raheem Mostert #31 of the Miami Dolphins is tackled by Jordan Hicks #58 of the Minnesota Vikings during the second quarter at Hard Rock Stadium on October 16, 2022 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Megan Briggs/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings return home to U.S. Bank Stadium on Sunday to face a 0-3 Miami Dolphins team looking ahead to the 2027 NFL Draft. Their best offensive player, De’Von Achane, is officially out for the year with a torn ACL suffered last week. The Dolphins are tied for the league low with 36 points and have an abysmal -50 point differential. The next worst is the Green Bay Packers at -35. That’s a shame. Other than the Raiders, the Dolphins are probably my favorite AFC team, which makes it sad to see them circling the drain so early in the 2026 season. The NFL seems better when these legacy franchises do well. Whether they’re on a “March for Arch,” “Tanking for Trinidad,” or looking elsewhere, like WR Jeremiah Smith, I hope it works out for them. Whenever the Dolphins visit Minneapolis every eight years, I’m reminded of one of my favorite NFL regular-season games ever from 1994. It was a wild game. Coincidentally, it was also played in Week 4. The Vikings went up 28-0 as Warren Moon and the Vikings offense rolled, and the defense intercepted Dan Marino three times. But, of course, since we are the Vikings, nothing is ever easy. Ever. Marino went berserk and tied the game at 28-28. Moon and company made enough plays down the stretch to hold on for a 38-35 victory. We’ve gone from Moon and Marino combining for 757 passing yards to Malik Willis and a Vikings offense that feels like it won’t reach 757 passing yards for the rest of the season. Will this be the week the offense finally shows signs of life? VIKINGS ON OFFENSE If Kevin O’Connell and the Vikings’ passing game can’t make hay at home this week (Justin Jefferson or not), it may be time to dust off the panic button. The Dolphins are 28th in points allowed, 32nd in opponents’ completion percentage, 31st in QB pressures, and 32nd in sacks. They have zero sacks so far in the 2026 season. Yes, zero. The Dolphins rank a respectable 12th in the NFL in rush yards allowed, but that may be because teams find it easier to get to the scoreboard through the air. This defense is giving up completions at an astonishing 80.3% clip. That’s really bad, folks. This parade of statistical ineptitude will put enormous pressure on KOC, Kyler Murray, and the passing offense in a get-right game. If not now, when? Seriously. With Aaron Jones not 100%, Jordan Mason on IR, and no one else averaging more than 3.3 yards per carry, it feels like the time to look more like the 1998 Vikings than the 2012 version (in the first half, anyway). Given the numbers, it should be a case of “No Jefferson? No problem” for KOC and company. It better be. If not, it may be fair to ask what exactly was going on all spring and summer. VIKINGS ON DEFENSE I suspect a shipment of Excedrin Extra Strength and Pepto Bismol was dumped in front of offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik’s office this week. He’ll need it. Without their premier offensive weapon (Achane), he now faces Brian Flores and a Vikings defense that is allowing only 13.7 points per game. Oh, and it’s also ranked 1st in sacks, 1st in QB hits, 1st in fewest points per drive, 1st in DVOA, and 1st in EPA. So far, the Dolphins offense has struggled: 31st in points per game (12.0), 26th in total yards, and 25th in sacks taken. They’re a bit better in passing and rushing yards per game (20th in each) and in yards per play (19th). I’m a fan of Malik Willis and think he can be a good NFL starter, but so far things haven’t gone well. He’s currently 29th in passer rating and 27th in QBR. He has very little help, which is a big reason for these numbers. Hey, as a Vikings supporter, I’m not gonna sit here and make jokes about a team’s poor offensive stats, since 200 passing yards for us is the football equivalent of scaling Mount Everest with your hands and feet tied together. That said, we’re not the ones about to enter Flores’ house of horrors, either. It won’t be a treat, I can guarantee. FearFest may be on AMC all of October, but for one afternoon it’s taking a detour through U.S. Bank Stadium. PREDICTION If the Vikings don’t shoot themselves in the foot with turnovers or poor special teams play, I’m having a hard time seeing how the Dolphins can even score 10 points on us, let alone multiple touchdowns. If KOC and the offensive coaches can’t figure out a way to make the passing game look at least mediocre this week, I’ll be shocked. I expect Justin Jefferson to (wisely) sit this one out, but it shouldn’t matter. This has to be the time. I’m putting my money where my mouth is. I already had Kyler Murray as a backup in one fantasy league and picked him up after Week 1 in another. Drake Maye and Justin Herbert (don’t even get me started on that guy) are getting the boot. Jordan Addison will start on my one team, too. Let’s do this. Even if the Vikings’ offense wakes up this week, I’m still taking a wait-and-see approach before declaring the issue resolved. Things get tougher in a hurry, and I’ll have to see it against playoff-level competition before officially showing my buddy skepticism the door. But you have to start somewhere, right? Minnesota Vikings: 27 Miami Dolphins: 7

Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. title: Can Kevin O’Connell’s 3-0 Vikings Survive the Dolphins Trap? Week 4 Preview
summary: The 3-0 Minnesota Vikings face a Miami Dolphins team in full rebuild mode, but as The Real Forno Show warns, this Week 4 matchup has trap game written all over it. — Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano sat down with Dolphins guy Kevin Fielder for the Week 4 preview, and this one is messier than […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 27: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the game at Raymond James Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-0 Minnesota Vikings face a Miami Dolphins team in full rebuild mode , but as The Real Forno Show warns, this Week 4 matchup has trap game written all over it. — Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano sat down with Dolphins guy Kevin Fielder for the Week 4 preview, and this one is messier than a 7-point spread and actually it being double-digits. Miami, under Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley, is in an evaluation year. Not a tank. Fielder put it on Sullivan: “This is not going to be a rebuild in the sense that we’re gonna tear this down.” They brought in Malik Willis to reunite him with two people who already coached him in Green Bay. Early returns are mixed. Fielder was honest about it: “I think we’ll be talking about the Miami Dolphins needing a quarterback at some point in the next few years.” De’Von Achane tore his ACL in Week 3, so Bobby Slowik has to rebuild the run game around Ollie Gordon and Jaylen Wright. The Vikings have their own questions. Kyler Murray has one full game in purple. Justin Jefferson had not practiced all week when we recorded. Tyler watched that debut and said, “I think he saw too much flash of color and decided not to” throw it into those windows. Fielder pushed back: “He’s just missing things down the field… there were explosive plays to be had.” Brian Flores’ defense is going to test that Miami line. Fielder likes the interior: “Kadyn Proctor at left guard, Jonah Savaiinaea at right guard, Aaron Brewer at center, has played incredibly well.” The Vikings’ run game is still a work in progress with Josh Oliver out for the year and Aaron Jones always nicked up. Spread says comfortable. The tape says do not overlook them. Key Points from the Episode: The Dolphins are the NFL’s youngest roster but have been “oddly competitive” — pushing the Chiefs, 49ers, and Raiders De’Von Achane’s ACL injury forces a schematic shift toward power-gap running Chop Robinson, drafted to be a pass rusher, has struggled in year three — “he just has to figure something out” Miami’s defense is 30th in EPA per play and 32nd in EPA per dropback, but 9th against the run Brian Flores’ “blitz” numbers are inflated — his base is five rushers, which the NFL counts as a blitz complains Fielder Kyler Murray’s misses against Tampa were reads, not accuracy: “He’s missing things that he should be taking” If Justin Jefferson sits, Jordan Addison and Tai Felton take on larger roles Donovan Jackson has been a revelation at left guard: “That guy is a baller. I was wrong,” Fielder conceded Fielder called this the “quintessential trap game” — closer than fans expect Dave Stefano invoked the 2018 Bills upset: “We were so much favored and we got our [back sides] handed to us” Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The Real Forno Show is your go-to Minnesota Vikings podcast for film-room analysis, draft talk, and unfiltered takes — and this Week 4 preview is essential listening before kickoff. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano leave no angle uncovered, from Brian Flores’ defensive wizardry to the Kyler Murray chemistry clock ticking toward a Week 6 bye. Whether the Vikings roll or the Dolphins shock the world, this is the conversation that frames your Sunday. Fan with Us!!! Guest Kevin Fielder @TheKevinFielder joins Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . So here’s a question for you: Will the Vikings prove they can dominate a team they should beat, or is this the week Miami steals one nobody saw coming?

title: Patriots worried about ‘second play’ with Bills QB Josh Allen
summary: Josh Allen’s status as one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL is undisputed. What makes him such a dangerous and productive player is not just his arm talent, size and versatility, but how he uses a combination of his rare skills to become arguably the most frustration-inducing player in all of pro football. As […]
full_text: Josh Allen’s status as one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL is undisputed. What makes him such a dangerous and productive player is not just his arm talent, size and versatility, but how he uses a combination of his rare skills to become arguably the most frustration-inducing player in all of pro football. As long as he has the ball, after all, the Buffalo Bills have a chance. And the 30-year-old is making sure to keep that chance alive for as long as he can on every single play. This, in turn, puts immense pressure on opponents to keep defending even when a play otherwise would be long over. It is precisely what the New England Patriots have been harping on all week. “He’s going to extend plays. We know that’s going to happen. You can’t necessarily stop it, you only can contain it,” said safety Kevin Byard. “As DBs, we have to be able to cover for as long as it takes. Ten seconds — it doesn’t matter. Especially on the backend, it’s not necessarily the play that’s called, it’s the second or third play within the play. So, we’re going to have to be very mentally, but more than likely physically exhausted in this game because this team and Josh, they have no quit.” Defending the “second play” has been the Patriots’ defensive theme of the week. On the flip side, making said play has been Allen’s bread and butter since entering the NFL as a first-round draft choice out of Wyoming in 2018. The touchdown got wiped away by a hold on a downfield block, but Josh Allen doing this to you on fourth down must be the worst feeling ever. pic.twitter.com/yImsqnsymF — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) September 28, 2026 “It’s kind of like recess football in terms of, ‘If you have a man, you have to cover your man. And if you’re free, then you have to figure out a way to get this guy with the ball either down or out of bounds,’” said Patriots cornerbacks coach Justin Hamilton. “He’s elite, and he’s as good as I can remember seeing in my lifetime. I’ve watched a lot of NFL football. I don’t know of a guy that’s better at play extension.” Allen is able to make the so-called second plays because of his size, strength and vision. He can simply evade pressure or fight through tackle attempts, all while keeping his eyes downfield for either a rushing lane or receiver to open up downfield. This is why he is typically ranked high in time-to-throw metrics and also one of the most effective scrambling quarterbacks in the league. None of that is nothing new, of course. Defending it still remains a challenge, though — one the Patriots are going up against twice a year, including this coming Sunday. “It’s the hardest thing, in my opinion, in football to have to defend,” said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr, who referred to Allen as an “MVP-caliber quarterback playing MVP football.” For him, the secret to countering the extended play lies in the preparation. The goal is not just to know what is going to happen, but be capable of reacting in an instant without much hesitation. Kuhr used two words to describe the approach: muscle memory. “We try to rep it in practice. Tommy [DeVito] and Behren [Morton] are giving good looks,” he said. “We talk about our rules within it and we harp on it every single day, we show the film of it. Everybody’s got to know it. Everybody’s got to be on the same page. Everybody’s got to understand it, so it becomes muscle memory because he’s a special cat and he’s a different cat. You know you get to see that twice a year and it just looks different, so we have to do everything we can to make how we execute the second play muscle memory. “There can’t be any lapses of, ‘I thought the play was over.’ No, the play is never over. We have to do it for 60 minutes too — that’s the hardest part: this guy does not go away. No matter what the score is, he does not go away. So, we have to have the competitive stamina for 60 minutes, understand what our rules are to defend the second play, and we all have to be on the same page doing it, make it muscle memory.” Muscle memory is one part, game-day execution another. And for the Patriots, the latter will be difficult this week given their personnel situation. Two of their best defenders, cornerback Christian Gonzalez and defensive tackle Christian Barmore, will miss the contest on Sunday due to shoulder injuries. Under normal circumstances both would play valuable roles in keeping Allen contained through tight coverage and resetting the line of scrimmage, respectively. Without those blue-chip players, the task will be even more daunting than it already is. “It’s going to be a 60-minute ball game,” said Byard. “We could be up 35 points and he’s going to find a way to try to come back and score 40 points. This is going to be a tough challenge for us and we’re going to have to play a 60-minute complete ball game.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: How the Patriots plan to replace Christian Gonzalez against the Bills
summary: The New England Patriots’ task against the unbeaten Buffalo Bills this week has gotten significantly tougher. Christian Gonzalez, the team’s top cornerback and best overall player this season, has officially been ruled out of the contest due to a shoulder injury sustained last week. Gonzalez’s deactivation does not come as a surprise after he missed […]
full_text: The New England Patriots’ task against the unbeaten Buffalo Bills this week has gotten significantly tougher. Christian Gonzalez, the team’s top cornerback and best overall player this season, has officially been ruled out of the contest due to a shoulder injury sustained last week. Gonzalez’s deactivation does not come as a surprise after he missed the entire week of practice. It nonetheless forces the Patriots to adapt and replace one of the best defenders in the NFL. How are they going to do it? According to head coach Mike Vrabel, by relying on a mix of players. “I think Charles [Woods] will get some snaps in there,” Vrabel said during a press conference at Gillette Stadium on Friday. “We’ll mix around some guys. Marcus [Jones] will play outside, inside a little bit. I think Karon [Prunty]’s done a really nice job on special teams and so if he’s asked to play on defense, he’ll be ready to go.” Another member of the Patriots’ cornerback group, rookie Channing Canada, is questionable for the game with a hamstring injury. As for Gonzalez, his presence typically allows the Patriots to be aggressive with their coverage and pressure calls. The 2023 first-round draft pick, who became the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history last month, has proven himself capable of taking on opposing wide receivers in 1-on-1 coverage while also performing at a high level as a zone defender. The Patriots not having him available against one of the top offenses in the league and MVP-caliber quarterback Josh Allen naturally changes their plans. “There might be specific things if he’s not out there that maybe we do or don’t do,” explained defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr earlier this week. “You always have a plan in your mind for anybody. When we meet as a staff, every week — even Week 1 and we’re fully healthy — it’s like, ‘Okay, what if so and so goes down? What are we thinking here? How are we going to adjust that? Who are we going to move here?’ We talk about that every week, and you try to stay within the game plan you have in the week.” With Gonzalez out, New England’s game plan against Allen and company might look different than it otherwise would have. What definitely will be different is the defense’s overall quality with him not on the field, especially considering that stalwart defensive tackle Christian Barmore is also out. Even so, the team won’t take a defeatist attitude into Buffalo and has confidence in its abilities to pull off an upset win . “Gonzo’s a playmaker for sure, so we know we’re going to miss him out there. But we preach all the time, ‘next man up,’” said Carlton Davis. “Charles Woods has been playing well every time he had to step in for one of us. We’re going to trust him and go up to this game trying to win.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Patriots make decision on starting right guard vs. Bills
summary: For a second straight week, the New England Patriots had to find a new starting right guard. It looks like they have found one. Ben Brown, who spent last week’s game in Jacksonville as backup left guard and center, is slated to take over the position on Sunday against the Buffalo Bills. Patriots head coach […]
full_text: For a second straight week, the New England Patriots had to find a new starting right guard. It looks like they have found one. Ben Brown, who spent last week’s game in Jacksonville as backup left guard and center, is slated to take over the position on Sunday against the Buffalo Bills. Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said so during a press conference at Gillette Stadium on Friday. “I would probably anticipate Ben Brown starting out there,” Vrabel said. Brown, who spoke about his readiness should he be called upon earlier this week, will become the Patriots’ third different starting right guard in just four games this week. The position was originally occupied by Mike Onwenu, the team’s longest-tenured player, before a broken ankle forced him out of New England’s Week 2 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers. Veteran training camp pickup Greg Van Roten entered the lineup in Onwenu’s place, but was himself hurt the previous game versus the Jaguars. Both of them have since been placed on injured reserve, creating a vacancy at the position. Walter Rouse was the first man up to fill it last week, but the late-August trade acquisition via Minnesota struggled in his regular season debut with the team. As a consequence, the team held an open competition during practice leading up to the Bills game, featuring Brown, Rouse and recent signing Matt Pryor . And while the 28-year-old Brown will be the right guard in Buffalo, the other two could also factor into the mix at some point. “I think Walter will have to be ready to go,” said Mike Vrabel. “I think that we will see where we are with Matt Pryor coming over from Arizona, whether we feel like he could potentially help us at the game or be available for the game. I think that’s something that we still have to decide here as he works into the communication, the system, going on the road, and then if not, we’ll have to look to elevate somebody potentially.” The Patriots’ Week 4 game against the Bills is set for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff on Sunday.

Fullback Reggie Gilliam, tight end Eli Raridon, offensive tackle Morgan Moses, linebackers Dre’Mont Jones and Christian Elliss, cornerback Channing Canada and safety Craig Woodson since been called questionable to play. OUT Patriots DT Christian Barmore (shoulder) CB Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) S Brenden Schooler (back — NFI return ) Bills No players listed Early in last Sunday’s 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, Gonzalez had his shoulder examined by the training staff after a making a hard tackle on third down. No injury designation was announced after the defense got off the field. From there, the 2023 draft choice, 2024 All-Pro and 2025 Pro Bowler stayed in to see 52 out of 59 snaps for a cornerback depth chart that also includes Carlton Davis III, Charles Woods, Marcus Jones, Karon Prunty and the questionable Canada on the 53-man roster. No. 0 closed out September with eight tackles and five passes defensed. But back-to-back-to-back absences followed heading into the divisional matchup. title: NFL predictions: Will the Patriots upset the Bills in Week 4?
summary: Arguably the most impactful win of the New England Patriots’ 2025 season came against their biggest rivals. In Week 5, they managed to upset the Buffalo Bills 23-20 in primetime — a win that ended up setting the tone for the rest of the season, and for the AFC East title returning to Foxborough for […]
full_text: Arguably the most impactful win of the New England Patriots’ 2025 season came against their biggest rivals. In Week 5, they managed to upset the Buffalo Bills 23-20 in primetime — a win that ended up setting the tone for the rest of the season, and for the AFC East title returning to Foxborough for the first time in six years. Fast forward to 2026, and the Bills and their 3-0 record again look like a serious contender for the division title. The Patriots, on the other hand, are facing an uphill battle: not only did they start the season 1-2, their offense around MVP runner-up Drake Maye has struggled playing consistent football and holding onto the ball. If there ever was a get-right game for the team, this week’s might be it. The Patriots, after all, are headed to Buffalo for a rematch of that Week 5 battle last season. Will the outcome be the same this time around, and the 6.5-point underdogs according to FanDuel Sportsbook manage another upset in Orchard Park? Let’s find out what Pats Pulpit’s staff and community think. Patriots vs. Bills score predictions Bernd Buchmasser: The Patriots have had their fair share of struggles and will be heading into a hostile environment on Sunday. An upset would be monumental and, just like last year, might have a lasting effect on the team and it’s confidence. However, unlike in 2025, the gap between them and the Bills feels very much too big to be overcome at this point in time. While the game should be more competitive than last week’s shellacking in Jacksonville, New England’s issues and injury woes will be too much to overcome versus one of the best teams in the NFL. | Patriots 17, Bills 21 Patriots fans, join the game-day huddle! title: Ben Brown ‘ready to roll’ should Patriots call upon him against Bills
summary: Entering 2026, right guard was supposed to be a position of strength for the New England Patriots. Mike Onwenu had been their best offensive linemen for several years now, and even with plenty of football under his belt has remained a top-tier if somewhat underrated blocker in the run and pass game. However, three games […]
full_text: Entering 2026, right guard was supposed to be a position of strength for the New England Patriots. Mike Onwenu had been their best offensive linemen for several years now, and even with plenty of football under his belt has remained a top-tier if somewhat underrated blocker in the run and pass game. However, three games into the season the outlook has changed dramatically. Onwenu suffered a fractured ankle in Week 2 against Pittsburgh, with his replacement — training camp free agency pickup Greg Van Roten — going down with an ankle injury one week later. With both now on injured reserve, the Patriots are scrambling for answers at the spot. Looking at the roster, there are three candidates to fill Onwenu’s shoes now that Van Roten is out of the equation for at least four weeks: Ben Brown, Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor. Brown entered training camp as the No. 4 interior lineman but was hampered by an ankle injury in preseason; Rouse was acquired in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings ahead of late-August’s roster cutdowns; Pryor was signed just this week to provide additional depth and experience. Who among them will emerge as the starter remains to be seen, but based on past performance in the system, Brown looks like a realistic candidate. If indeed called upon, he vows to be ready. “Physically, I feel great. I’m ready to roll however that might look,” he said earlier this week. “It’s just like Coach [Mike Vrabel] always says, ‘Prepare every week as a starter regardless of if you’re actually out there or not.’ That’s what we are intending, to be ready. And so, whatever is asked upon me, I’ll be ready for whatever.” A rookie free agent in 2022, Brown made his way to New England via the Raiders practice squad in 2024. Since then, he has played 33 games with 14 starts — all of them at either left guard or center. In fact, only 11 of his 1,007 offensive snaps with the team have come at right guard. And yet, Brown feels confident in his ability to play that role, in part because he did so during his college career at Ole Miss. Ultimately, though, his goal is to just help the team regardless of the role he is asked to play on game days. “I want to do whatever I can to contribute, however that might look,” he said. “I just want to be ready for whenever my number’s called upon. Whenever that might be, because you never know in the NFL. It’s long seasons and a lot goes on in it. Best thing I can do for this football team is just be ready whenever my number’s called.”

title: Patriots mailbag: What’s wrong with the run game?
summary: The New England Patriots are looking to put a blowout loss behind them as they get ready for a big divisional battle against Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. I know it is early but I thought we would see improvements in the run game with the […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are looking to put a blowout loss behind them as they get ready for a big divisional battle against Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. I know it is early but I thought we would see improvements in the run game with the addition of Gilliam. An improved run game would certainly be a big plus while Maye figures things out. Why do you think we haven’t seen the positive impact yet of having a proven FB? The OL injuries? – sqpondme Why no outside runs utilizing Henderson’s speed? – Davel The Patriots’ run game has been poor for the second straight season, currently ranking last in the league in success rate and 24th in Rush EPA. While the running backs and offensive line are not free of blame, the scheme has not helped by stressing defenses pre-snap with motion or other creativity. Instead, the Patriots have largely leaned on duo this season, hoping to move defenders off the line of scrimmage, but have repeatedly run into bodies as defensive fronts use line games up front to create disruption. McDaniels, however, believes there is still value in staying the course early in the season. “I think last year we went through a very similar stage where sticking with certain things was helpful for us,” Josh McDaniels said Thursday. “I’ve talked about this a lot in a running game, in training camp, you have X amount of practices in pads. If you do or don’t play in the preseason games, that is what it is, right? So, you have opportunities to work together in a physical environment. And I think sometimes, what I’ve seen in the last so many years is September and October end up being an extension of that for the run game especially, because double teams and pads on a 330 lb. human being, when you don’t do it over and over and over again daily sometimes it takes a few more repetitions to get good at it. “And so, whether it’s outside zones or toss cracks or double seam schemes or draws, whatever the scheme is, I think fitting runs and doing it with the proper technique and fundamentals takes some time in pads.” It’s not realistic for the Patriots to completely scrap their run-game scheme, meaning more time on task will need to produce better results. But there are ways New England could add more variety, including getting TreVeyon Henderson outside more often. Henderson has seen 37% of his carries outside the tackles this season, compared to 49% last season, albeit in a small sample size. There should be opportunities for him and Rhamondre Stevenson to hit the edges this week against the Bills defense. When it comes to Gilliam, the fullback is clearly hobbled which is affecting his playing time and impact. His workload was managed the entire offseason before he finally was listed on the injury report this week with a knee injury. What is going on with Hunter Henry and why has he disappeared? I said I think Eli Raridon could be TE #1 by season’s end. That might be sooner than even I thought. When should we expect Eli Raridon to return fully healthy? – For Pats Sake The lack of a true blocking tight end has also worked against them in the run game. As for Henry, the 31-year old certainly has appeared to lose a step early on, while teams are also sitting on his underneath routes in quick game concepts to take his production away. Raridon was back to being a limited participant this week so should be ready to go Sunday. The Patriots need him back on the field for his explosiveness in the passing game and blocking ability. What is the formula to restore Maye confidence – 7i165 Correcting Maye’s confidence, decisiveness and decision-making are the biggest things that need to improve for him to get back on track. As for how to do that, I’m not in Maye’s mind or a psychologist. That’s something for the coaching staff to figure out, which raises an interesting question: Should they rein him in and try to prevent him from beating himself? That brings risk in itself, as Maye could lose the aggressiveness that typically makes him so dangerous. If take away Maye’s turnovers, how would you rate him this year as a Quarterback? – sumeetw Analytically, Maye has been around league average when removing the six interceptions and one fumble. I’d say that passes the eye test as there are still encouraging signs on film such as him generating explosives against Pittsburgh, stepping up through the pocket in Jacksonville or working a scramble drill to Kyle Williams in the fourth quarter. He is also moving the football as the Patriots are 12th in the league in yards per drive. The turnovers and penalties are just not allowing them to finish, as they rank last in points per drive (0.97). Mike Onwenu, our starting Right Guard, goes onto to IR. A week later, Greg Van Roten, the top backup, joins him on IR. Walter Rouse replaced GVR, and he struggled in this new position for him. Is Rouse the answer going forward? Or would Ben Brown be a better option? – PatsFanFromNH I would go with Ben Brown. He’s proven to be their best interior backup and right guard is his natural position dating back to college. Whether that is a season-long fix or not is TBD, and I also wouldn’t rule out newly signed Matt Pryor factoring into the mix in some fashion. Is it too early to start thinking about who we should be looking at in next year’s draft? – poindexterregan It’s never too early to start thinking about next year’s draft. It should be a loaded class and I’d imagine the front seven will be an area of emphasis for the Patriots. I’m not ready to start thinking about some of the edge rushers projected in the top-five, but Georgia linebacker Chris Cole has been a favorite of mine as a mid-to-late first-round pick. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

title: Saints vs. Falcons: QB to QB Matchup
summary: The New Orleans Saints will see their bitter rivals enter the Superdom for a primetime matchup on Monday night as they face off against the Atlanta Falcons. The Falcons have been down on their luck, but they are certainly not lacking talent. Their offense still features some of the best young players in the league, […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough (6) is sacked by Detroit Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes (55) during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will see their bitter rivals enter the Superdom for a primetime matchup on Monday night as they face off against the Atlanta Falcons. The Falcons have been down on their luck, but they are certainly not lacking talent. Their offense still features some of the best young players in the league, including Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts. However, they just can’t seem to find consistency at the quarterback position. Throughout the offseason, there was a quarterback battle between Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa. Tua actually won the job while Penix continued to recover from an injury. However, before the first game of the season, Tua suffered an injury of his own. The Falcons then turned to Cooper Rush, who started in Week 1 and 2. With the offense struggling to perform, they turned to their fourth quarterback, Jack Strand, who came in and immediately threw a pick-six against the Panthers. Finally, last week, the Falcons were able to get Penix back, and the offense showed some life. Penix’s first drive of the season also ended with an interception, but after that, the Falcons were able to surprise a lot of people by defeating the Packers on the road, 35-14. Penix was Atlanta’s starting quarterback last year but struggled to find a rhythm. This could be the year he takes a step forward. In his lone start of the season, Penix completed 18 of 25 passes (72%) for 256 yards, averaging 10.2 yards per attempt, with one touchdown and one interception. The good news for the Falcons is that they did not allow a single sack against the Packers last week, and that is something the Saints will need to change. The focus for the Saints’ defense shouldn’t necessarily be to stop Penix. If anything, it should be to force Penix to be the one who has to beat them. Bijan Robinson went off against the Packers, rushing for 194 yards and two touchdowns, while Drake London complemented the running game with nine receptions for 194 yards. He also had a long reception of 68 yards. Most of Penix’s passing production came from one receiver, while Robinson accounted for much of the offense’s remaining production. The Saints will need to generate pressure up the middle. With Penix being a left-handed quarterback, the normal pass-rushing dynamics are flipped a little. His blind side is to his right, so the Saints need to prevent him from stepping up into his throws, especially considering that he isn’t much of a threat to run. Flush him out of the pocket and force him to change his throwing spots. They will also need to take away his first read, which is usually Drake London. Force the Falcons into third-and-long situations by getting to Robinson on early downs and keeping the offense off schedule. Last year, the Saints had success against Atlanta and Bijan Robinson’s rushing attack. In two games against the Saints, Brandon Staley’s defense held Robinson to a combined 103 rushing yards and zero touchdowns. So, it’s possible. Tyler Shough and the Saints’ Offense : Tyler Shough leads the Saints nto this matchup, and had the fourth quarter against the Raiders not been played, Shough would have been coming off the best game of his young career. But football is a four-quarter sport. Through the first three games, Shough has 912 passing yards and is completing 68.9% of his passes. He also has eight touchdowns and three interceptions. The most notable thing about Shough’s stat line is that the games in which he has committed a turnover are the games the Saints have lost. Start by protecting the football. The Saints also have to help him in that regard because the pass protection has been very poor. Through the first three games, Shough has been sacked 10 times. That’s not good for the offense, and it’s certainly not good to allow your starting quarterback to continue taking hits like that. The Saints will need to establish a running game around Shough on Monday night, and that challenge just got harder. Travis Etienne Jr. will miss some time after suffering a hamstring injury against the Raiders which means Kendre Miller and Alvin Kamara will become the focal points of the rushing attack. The Saints also did a great job utilizing their tight ends on Sunday, creating mismatches by incorporating more 12 personnel. Noah Fant and Juwan Johnson both played very well because of it. And, obviously, get the ball to Chris Olave. Olave is making a case to be the best receiver in the league right now, and the Saints need to continue featuring him in the offense. Find that Guardian Cap early and often on Monday night. Finally, encourage Shough to run. He has good mobility and can make a defense pay when its pass rushers become undisciplined. Encourage him to use his legs and make the defense think twice about sending blitzes. He can get rid of the ball quickly and extend plays with his feet. The Falcons have been able to generate pressure with just four rushers, so it will be important for Shough to make them pay whenever they decide to send more than that. The Matchup : When it comes to this matchup, the Saints have the advantage in talent at the quarterback position, while the Falcons have the advantage in the talent surrounding their quarterback. This is an important game because it’s a divisional matchup, and the Saints are coming off a loss. They can’t afford to lose games within the division if they want to have a chance at the postseason. The NFC South isn’t a particularly strong division, so the Saints need to come out and win. To do that, they must make sure they showcase that they have the better quarterback on the field Monday night. Who do you think has the advantage heading into this matchup, and how do you think this game will turn out?
author: Anthony Parker

title: Key matchups: Saints vs. Falcons
summary: The New Orleans Saints are honoring the 20th anniversary of their iconic Domecoming game with another Monday Night Football matchup against the Atlanta Falcons. The Domecoming game is the one of most emotional and significant moments in Saints history, and Monday is simply a game New Orleans needs to win. On top of being an […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints throws a pass against the Las Vegas Raiders during the first half of an NFL game on September 27. 2026, at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are honoring the 20th anniversary of their iconic Domecoming game with another Monday Night Football matchup against the Atlanta Falcons. The Domecoming game is the one of most emotional and significant moments in Saints history, and Monday is simply a game New Orleans needs to win. On top of being an NFC South matchup, the Domecoming reunion could either kick-start a big run for the Saints, or be the game we point to when it all goes wrong. The Saints need to take advantage of these pivotal matchups to come away with a win on Monday. Saints run defense vs. RB Bijan Robinson The strength of the Falcons is clearly superstar running back Bijan Robinson. The fourth-year running back has been unstoppable since entering the league and is at the peak of his prime. While Robinson is one of the premier players in the NFL, the Falcons’ offense is significantly lacking. Part of the Falcons ‘ shortcomings is their lack of talent at quarterback. Despite Michael Penix Jr. having a solid day in the upset win over the Green Bay Packers, the way to stop Atlanta is slowing down Robinson. The Falcons have the second-best rushing offense in the league and a favorable matchup against the Saints’ run defense, which is ranked the sixth-worst in the NFL. Slowing down Robinson will be difficult, but will prove to be worthwhile, forcing Atlanta’s bottom-five passing offense to beat them in the air. Saints RBs vs. Falcons run defense Running back Travis Etienne Jr. finally started to look promising after a slow start to the season, but left during the team’s Week 3 loss with a hamstring injury. After further testing, it was determined Etienne’s injury was significant enough, and he was placed on injured reserve. With Etienne out, the offense looks towards veterans Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller. The Saints’ run offense has been awful this season. Tyler Shough has been forced to throw 132 passes through three games, and it has not been sustainable. On top of his 132 pass attempts, the lack of a run game has allowed teams to blitz Shough at a high rate. Part of the Saints’ failures to run the ball has been the poor play design. New Orleans’ run game isn’t creative and doesn’t utilize their backs’ strengths. Kellen Moore clearly knows what it’s like to run a successful rushing offense, but it has not followed him to New Orleans. But getting the run game going on Monday will be the Saints’ offense’s strongest matchup yet. Surprisingly, the Falcons have the best run defense in the NFL, allowing just 47.7 rushing yards per game. QB Tyler Shough vs. Falcons secondary Tyler Shough had a career game against the Las Vegas Raiders, and it would look a lot better if you just turned a blind eye to what happened in the fourth quarter. Obviously, however, the fourth-quarter meltdown can’t be ignored. But Shough may be in for another career day against Atlanta. While they house the best run defense in the NFL, the Falcons also have the fourth-worst passing defense and are now without their star cornerback, A.J. Terrell Jr. With Chris Olave’s big season continuing and Shough coming off a big day, New Orleans could take advantage of a favorable matchup.

title: Saints draft position: Entering Week 4
summary: After a loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, the New Orleans Saints’ draft pick position has shifted significantly. Instead of selecting near the playoff section, they are back in the top-10, right where they selected two seasons ago. Here are two prospects that the Saints could select at pick 9: Georgia CB Ellis Robinson IV […]
full_text: ATHENS, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 26: KJ Bolden #4 of the Georgia Bulldogs rushes after an interception during the second quarter against the Oklahoma Sooners at Sanford Stadium on September 26, 2026 in Athens, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, the New Orleans Saints’ draft pick position has shifted significantly. Instead of selecting near the playoff section, they are back in the top-10, right where they selected two seasons ago. Here are two prospects that the Saints could select at pick 9: Georgia CB Ellis Robinson IV The first player we will talk about is Ellis Robinson IV. If the Saints are unable to upgrade the edge position early in the draft, CB has to be the next best option. These two position groups benefit from each other the most on defense. If the DBs cover well, it allows an average pass rush to get to the QB, but if you have a great pass rush, it stops the pass defense from getting picked apart. The Saints do not have a good pass rush or a good CB room. Kool-Aid McKinstry has played pretty well so far, and Quincy Riley has made some plays, but this team does not have a clear CB1. Robinson can be that player. He is great in both man and zone coverage, is physical, and has his eyes on the ball for a turnover. The issue is that his focus on getting an interception can cause him to get beat, which is a worry. Georgia SAF KJ Bolden Sticking with the DBs and Georgia, another player that would make sense is safety KJ Bolden, but some things need to happen first. If the Saints want to keep Jonas Sanker at slot, which hasn’t been horrible, then safety can become a major position of need. So far, since signing Justin Reid, it hasn’t been great. Not bad, but not the level of safety that I think many of us expected. His leadership has been great, and I do think that’s important, but is it crazy to say the Saints could move on from him this offseason? A post-June 1st cut would be a low dead cap hit and save some money. Even if the Saints do not move on from Reid, they will need to add a safety this season, but if they release their captain, Bolden would make a ton of sense. At Georgia, Bolden has been an incredible run defender and tackler, while also providing flexibility around the defense, and has become a leader for the Bulldogs. Bolden is a clear upgrade who could be sitting there at pick 9.

title: If Saints win/lose vs. Falcons
summary: After a gut-punching defeat to the Las Vegas Raiders at the weekend, the New Orleans Saints are gearing up to host the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football in a huge divisional matchup. Here’s what either result could mean for the black and gold. If the Saints win: All games matter, and all divisional games […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - SEPTEMBER 27: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints speaks to his teammates before kickoff against the Las Vegas Raiders during an NFL football game at Cesars Superdome on September 27, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a gut-punching defeat to the Las Vegas Raiders at the weekend, the New Orleans Saints are gearing up to host the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football in a huge divisional matchup. Here’s what either result could mean for the black and gold. If the Saints win: All games matter, and all divisional games matter that little bit more. But this particular clash has all the ingredients to be particularly season-defining at an early stage. The Saints have categorically played better than their record shows. Getting back to .500 and winning their first NFC South matchup of the season is absolutely crucial, and would allow the black and gold to almost start afresh, likely atop the division, and put some of the bad luck of the opening few weeks behind them. In last week’s edition of this piece, some readers disagreed with me for labeling Week 4 a must-win in the event that New Orleans lost to Las Vegas. Unfortunately, that scenario is upon us. And it does indeed feel like must-win territory. But Kellen Moore’s squad can restore all of the feel good factor that came after the win in Baltimore by overcoming their divisional foes and improving to 2-2 on the year. If the Saints lose: A loss would be truly sickening for the black and gold. However, falling to 1-3 against the Falcons in this spot wouldn’t kill the chances of winning the division, far from it. But it would certainly nonetheless feel like a major setback. And to drop consecutive games in the Caesars Superdome to Las Vegas and Atlanta has to say something about the ceiling on this team, especially with another key injury to Travis Etienne Jr being added to the woes. Both defeats to date have felt harsh. New Orleans has good reason to feel hard done by. But losing to Atlanta on Monday night, even in its own right, would feel like a big disappointment. What are you expecting from the black and gold on primetime? How do you rate the Falcons after their surprise beatdown of Green Bay?

title: Giants vs. Cardinals: Which Arizona team is the real one?
summary: With the New York Giants facing the Arizona Cardinals this week we turn to Seth Cox of SB Nation’s Revenge of the Birds for our weekly ‘5 questions’ segment. Ed: Which is likely the more realistic version of the Cardinals. The team that lost 31-7 to the Seattle Seahawks or the team that pushed the […]
full_text: Jeremiyah Love taking the field. | Getty Images With the New York Giants facing the Arizona Cardinals this week we turn to Seth Cox of SB Nation’s Revenge of the Birds for our weekly ‘5 questions’ segment. Ed: Which is likely the more realistic version of the Cardinals. The team that lost 31-7 to the Seattle Seahawks or the team that pushed the San Francisco 49ers in a 36-30 loss? Seth: That is the million dollar question for the Arizona Cardinals. We knew the defense would be an issue, more on that later, but we expected a little more from the offense. The Cardinals threw the ball 52 times for 280 yards against the Niners. Again, the stats 280 yards and two passing touchdowns are good, but their pass game is basically a really good run game. They are the second-worst team in explosive plays and they almost play not to lose, as opposed to make big plays and put pressure on the opposition. It also tends to coincide with big deficits, so teams are willing to allow them to beat them with a death by thousand cuts, because it runs so much time and they know their own offense will go in and score immediately. Ed: The Giants drafted Saquon Barkley No. 2 overall in 2018, and as great as he was there were also mixed feelings about that. How do fans feel about the selection of Jeremiyah Love, and does it look like he will justify being the third overall pick in the draft? Seth: This is a little hard to explain. I think 95% of fans are positive in the sense that Jeremiyah Love was a blue chip prospect and looks like he will be very good to great in the NFL. However, I feel like it is 50/50 at best if fans agree with the usage of that pick for that position, when you are looking at maybe the worst defense in the NFL that is not actively trying to tank like the Dolphins. Arvell Reese, Sonny Styles, heck even Caleb Downs may have helped more in the immediate, but I don’t think that means anyone is overthinking it right now, but they are definitely going to continue to monitor things. Ed: If you could take one player off the Giants’ roster and put him in Arizona’s lineup, who would it be? Why? Seth: Well, now that Brian Burns is gone, I think it would be Jermaine Eluemunor. The Cardinals desperately need help at the right tackle position and Eluemunor has not only a claim as the best right tackle in the NFL, but maybe as the best tackle overall. That would help the above problem with the pick of Jeremiyah Love and the lack of explosive offensive plays… right? Ed: What are your early thoughts on Mike LaFleur as a head coach? Does he look like a guy who could be Arizona’s coach for a while? Seth: Unfortunately for the Cardinals, LaFleur is on the clock as soon as he starts. The average tenure of a Cardinals head coach since they moved to Arizona is three years. Not many coaches get past that, and the ones that do usually flame out very early into their second contract, if they even start that second contract. That being said, outside of procedural/pre-snap penalties, LaFleur looks more than capable of being a really good head coach in the NFL. So much so that you feel at times like this could be the coach that bucks the trend of misfortune for the Cardinals head coaches. But they need to clean things up, and then show they can compete within their own division for him to have any real shot as being the long-term answer. Ed: The Cardinals are a slight favorite. If the Giants are going to win, what would that look like? What weaknesses can the Giants exploit? Seth: Does your team have a quarterback/running back/offensive talent? If so, then this could be your lucky day, as the Cardinals defense has been mostly bad, and sometimes downright atrocious this season. Think about this stat from the Cardinals 36-30 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, the Cardinals ran 31 more plays and possessed the ball 17 more minutes than the Niners… and the 49ers outgained them by 72 yards. That is really unfathomable. So, if the Cardinals defense doesn’t find a way to slow down what has been an impotent offense of the Giants since the injury to Jaxson Dart, I don’t know how they can stop any team’s offense. And also, I don’t see them stopping the Giants offense. They did okay against the Chargers, but I think with how well the Giants are coached, and how much they can run the ball, something the Cardinals cannot stop, it will be an interesting game. Stop the short passes by Jacoby Brissett, make him stand in the pocket and try and push the ball down the field and live with the results. On offense, hand the ball to Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris and work the play action game. If you do all of that, the game will be competitive and the Giants as home dogs may look silly. Good luck and good health in this one.
author: Ed Valentine

title: New York Giants mailbag: J.J. McCarthy, cornerback help, Arvell Reese, more
summary: Lawrence Kenney asks: With the trade for McCarthy, we assume his rookie contract, but does it include his option year? Assuming we can help rehabilitate his career, this could be an attractive trade chip.  Ed says: Yes, the Giants also get the fifth-year option. It is part of the standard rookie contract for first-round picks. […]
full_text: Lawrence Kenney asks: With the trade for McCarthy, we assume his rookie contract, but does it include his option year? Assuming we can help rehabilitate his career, this could be an attractive trade chip. Ed says: Yes, the Giants also get the fifth-year option. It is part of the standard rookie contract for first-round picks. Jim Eggers asks: Please explain to me how Nubin can look so absolutely clueless playing safety in the NFL. He had a great college career at Minnesota. Senior year 1st team All American with 13 career interceptions and was a tackling machine. A plug and play guy for sure, right. Not exactly. In the NFL he has no coverage skills, he is very slow, no situational awareness, just overmatched. No coaching will help this guy. Ed says: Jim, I think you are being a bit harsh. Tyler Nubin has clearly not been the player the Giants hoped he would be when they drafted him. He has been below average, and has not been the ball-hawking playmaker the Giants thought they were getting. You make it seem as though he doesn’t belong in the league. I’m not willing to go there. Rob Stolzer asks: With Burns now out for the year, will we be seeing Reese shifted over to the edge position for more plays? Ed says: Rob, it is an option. Pro Football Focus says Reese has aligned outside on 30 of 177 snaps (16.9%). Maybe that ticks up some based on situations. There have been times when Reese and Abdul Carter have switches, simply to get Carter pass rushing over a guard. Reese, though, will remain primarily an inside linebacker. Honestly, the pass rush remains an underdeveloped area of Reese’s game. Per PFF, he has rushed just 17 times so far. His 5.9% pressure rate is 137th out of 200 grades off-ball linebackers or edge defenders. That is a small sample size, but perhaps an indication that Reese is a work in progress as a pass rusher. I think the Giants signed Jihad Ward to be their third edge defender. Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, I probably missed it but I don’t remember much hype about Holland in the off season other than the Leadership Council and the contract extension. There were other players (e.g. Carter, Reese, and Sisi) I remember people talking about but not so much Holland. He’s emerging as a leader on and off the field. What did I miss? Ed says: Kölner, you didn’t miss anything. Holland didn’t make a lot of plays for the Giants a year ago, and since his career-high in interceptions for a season was two entering this year there was doubt he would become a big-time playmaker. Well, he has. Chase Baldwin asks: We traded for J.J. McCarthy in the wake of this I saw BBV split between this is horrendous, and he’ll be taking over starting soon. A few people sat in the middle and think he’s a fine #2. My question is word got out Monday afternoon, J.J. has to get from Minnesota to NY what does that look like ? Does he just hop on a plane with a few belongings and ship his stuff to NY? Do teams trading a player usually give them a heads up it could happen and to maybe pack up their things ? Just curious about the logistics of him actually getting settled in NY. Ed says: Chase, per the Collective Bargaining Agreement, teams are required to pay travel and moving expenses when they acquire a player. Teams also generally provide players with short-term living arrangements until they are able to find their own places. Teams often help arrange travel plans for new players. Players find out about trades when they get traded. Teams don’t give players a heads up that they might get traded, although players can often figure that out on their own. Chris Milner asks: What’s your sense of the progress that the Giants are making in building a playoff and championship contender? Are they moving the needle, or are they just struggling to get by with all the injuries? Ed says: Chris, the answer is actually in your question. They are “building” a championship contender. They are not, and never were going to be, a championship contender this year. The injuries put them in survivial mode for this season. But, the culture that has been established, the quality young players they have added, and what John Harbaugh learns about what this team needs going forward are all part of the process. Jason Zalewski asks: Why do you think we’ve been so poor at drafting early round CBs? Feels like we’ve been in CB purgatory since our SB wins. The jury is still out on Tae Banks. Ed says: Jason, have the Giants been bad at drafting early-round cornerbacks? It is way too early to judge Colton Hood. Dru Phillips, a third-round pick, is a good player. Cor’Dale Flott played well last year. It really isn’t fair to go back beyond Joe Schoen’s tenure as GM. Schoen has one miss in Banks, and even that might still be salvaged. Fletcher Wyman asks: Cutting through all the JJ noise and looking at a specific position of need I’ll ask you directly what you think of the possibility of trading for Riley Moss, mimicking a feed post I made today. He’s a 26yo starter that will be a UFA in 2027. He is very good against the run and plays opposite of Surtain so he’s targeted at a very high rate. He’s considered grabby but is middle of the pack for penalties vs targets. Denver may be interested in gaining assets before he has the opportunity to test the market. Ed says: Fletcher, I won’t claim to have studied Moss. The Broncos are a Super Bowl contender, though. Why would they trade a starting player off their defense when they are in win-now mode? I am in favor of adding good players. What’s the cost, financially and in draft capital? You don’t trade for him without giving him a long-term contract? Does acquiring him get in the way of letting Colton Hood develop? I’m not sure I see this one as realistic. Roy Koeslag asks: I know with all of the injuries to key players at the Giants, the thoughts on how we can solve the season must be ongoing. Trading for QB McCarthy seems like a risk because we don’t have a lot of picks next year. Signing a veteran QB with a similar profile as Dart would have been a better option in my opinion. Do you think they will try to add a veteran CB to help out? That seems like a much more urgent hole in our team. Ed says: Roy, the Giants traded for McCarthy because they believed he has more upside than anyone they could have signed as a free agent or taken off a practice squad. I appreciate the aggression. Will it pay off? Nobody knows. As for cornerback, I think it’s a wait-and-see deal. Can Greg Newsome keep playing well? What will Tae Banks provide when he is is healthy again? How will Colton Hood develop? Will Paulson Adebo help when he returns? I think the Giants need to be very careful about giving away draft assets. The focus still has to be on the future. Giving away assets that compromise the future for short-term fixes that — maybe — help you win one or two more games this year doesn’t seem like a good plan. Stephen Goodyear asks: Understand and agree with the aversion to a Porter acquisition. But it seems we have CB issues. First, injury updates on Adebo and Banks please? Secondly, Newsome seems OK. Holland seem positioned improve by playing. Then what? If either Holland or Newsome gets injured. Jones? Washington? Ed says: Another cornerback question. Stephen, I think Banks might play this weekend. Adebo is on IR. He can’t return until at least Week 6. I don’t know if he will. Jevon Holland is a safety, so he shouldn’t be part of the conversation. In the short term, I think the Giants just have to ride with Colton Hood and let him develop. He is being forced to play more than anticipated due to injuries. In the long run, that might help him. Could the Giants trade for a cornerback? If they do, I would think they would be looking for a player who would be a multi-year acquisition. They might just have to get by the best they can, and then try to address it in the offseason. Brian Scott asks: In past years we’ve seen various members of the front office — Joe Schoen and Brandon…
