title: Washington Commanders vs Indianapolis Colts Week 4: Five Questions with Stampede Blue
summary: It’s week 4 of the NFL season, and the 1-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 1-2 Indianapolis Colts team at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, England Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET. The Colts are in a bit of a similar situation as the Commanders. The Colts also started the season 0-2, losing to the […]
full_text: It’s week 4 of the NFL season, and the 1-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 1-2 Indianapolis Colts team at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, England Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET. The Colts are in a bit of a similar situation as the Commanders. The Colts also started the season 0-2, losing to the Ravens in week 1 and the Chiefs in week 2, before winning an upset victory in week 3 against their division-rivals, the Houston Texans. The Colts coaching staff also find themselves on the hotseat and might consider this a must-win game despite how early it is in the season. On offense, the Colts are coached by HC Shane Steichen and OC Jim Bob Cooter, both of whom have been running the Colts offense since 2023. Washington fans may remember Steichen for his time as OC of the Philadelphia Eagles from 2021-2022. From his time with the Eagles and through to the Colts, Steichen has run a primarily shotgun-based offense ( 55.6% shotgun rate ) that makes heavy use of under-center formation and play action ( 20.3% play action rate, 3rd-highest in the NFL ). It’s hard to describe Steichen’s offense as it’s not exactly a West Coast offense and it doesn’t exactly fit into the mold of other offenses. Steichen’s offense is really a deceptively simple, yet flexible offense that attempts to create a lot of options from the same looks. It builds in lots of layers in the passing game, so that QBs have options to throw it to all levels of the field depending on what coverage is called. Its foundation is the run game, built around RB Jonathan Taylor, who combines track-star speed (running a 4.39 40-time) and elite tackle-breaking agility and power. The success of the run game sets up the play-action passing game, freezing pass rushers long enough to allow QB Daniel Jones to make deep throws all over the field. However, the Colts vertical passing game will be hindered with the loss of WR Alec Pierce to injury, as he was their primary field stretcher. Without Pierce, the Colts passing game has largely funneled through WR Josh Downs, who only received 4 targets in week 1 alongside a healthy Alec Pierce, but has received a shocking 20 targets over weeks 2 & 3 with Alec Pierce sidelined. Downs lines up primarily in the slot, so his potential matchup on CB Mike Sainristil will be something to monitor. On defense, the Colts are in their second season with DC Lou Anarumo, former longtime DC of the Bengals. Nominally, Anarumo runs a 4-3 defense, though in reality he makes heavy use of variable fronts and disguises. The Colts DL is headlined by former All-Pro DT DeForest Buckner and 2024 1st-round pick DE Laiatu Latu (who had 8.5 sacks last season). Anarumo had a DB coaching background before being elevated to coordinator, which shows in his variable coverage structures and heavy use of disguise and last-minute rotations in coverage. Anarumo’s defense ends up in man coverage at a 30.1% rate, 3rd-highest in the NFL . The problem with man coverage is it only works as well as its weakest link, so it requires multiple DBs who are good in man coverage. I think this is the reason the Colts signed former All-Pro CB Charvarius Ward in the 2025 offseason and traded two 1st-round picks for repeat All-Pro CB Ahmad “Sauce” Gardner during the 2025 season, probably believing that the latter would solidify the secondary. Unfortunately, that has not come to fruition, as teams continue to pick on the other weak links in the Colts secondary, primarily in the middle of the field. The result is a defense that has allowed the 3rd-most passing yards and 4th-most rushing yards through three games this year. A big part of the problem with this defense has been missed tackles . The Colts had 9 missed tackles against the Ravens in week 1 and 19 (!!) missed tackles against the Chiefs in week 2, before dropping down to 4 missed tackles against the Texans in week 3. It remains to be seen if the improvement in week 3 is a trend or a fluke. I asked Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue five questions to better understand the state of the Colts and what to look for in this game. 1) The Colts defense gave up more than 500 yards in each of their first two games, but managed to hold the Texans to 223 yards and 17 points. What did the Colts do more effectively on defense last week and do you think the defense will stay improved going forward or was last week more about the Texans struggles on offense? The Colts defense underwent some big changes this offseason jettisoning long time defensive leaders, Zaire Franklin and Kenny Moore. Fans were largely tired of Franklin’s on and off field antics and most believed Moore’s best days were behind him. Ultimately it was the right move to attempt a soft reset on a defensive leadership group that had yet to find any sort of sustained success. They remade the linebacker corps with a mix of rookies and mid to low tier free agent additions. They replaced Nick Cross with third round rookie AJ Halucy and overhauled the defensive line rotation. Ultimately, it’s going to take time for this defense to find their footing. Sunday was a good showing, no doubt. They did a great job stopping the run and rushing CJ Stroud, but I believe their success had more to do with Houston’s offensive ineptitude than it marking some sort of tide turning moment for the Indy defense. Each week we should see the defense make incremental improvements before finally getting up to speed around week 8 or 9. I will be skeptical until they perform well against a quality offensive opponent. 2) What is your opinion of Daniel Jones and is he the future of the franchise? By the way, when Jones was on the Giants, he always played his best games against Washington, so I’m not looking forward to this matchup. Daniel Jones is the guy Indy should have had starting at quarterback when they drafted Anthony Richardson. Jones is a fine quarterback when surrounded by a good supporting cast and good play caller/offensive system. You’ll win games with him, not because of him. Meanwhile, if the supporting cast or play calling break down, he can lose you games without strong defensive performances, when he presses too hard or tries to force plays. Last week was the perfect encapsulation of who Jones is. He largely kept the offense moving, made some really good throws, stayed on schedule, made good checks at the line and kept things running smoothly for the majority of the game. He also threw a baffling interception and gave up two fumbles on avoidable strip sacks. If not for those three plays, Jones would have been great against a very good Texans defense. Instead Indy was fighting for its life inside of a minute to play in the fourth quarter. 3) What is your opinion of GM Chris Ballard and HC Shane Steichen? Ballard has been in position since 2017 and Steichen since 2023, yet neither has seen the Colts win the division in their tenure. I have a lot of sympathy for Ballard. In his first year as GM he had Josh McDaniels back out as his first head coaching hire (in hindsight this was a good thing, but it was highly embarrassing at the time) despite having already started to fill out McDaniels’ coaching staff and having several of his handpicked coaches already under contract. He believed he was walking into a situation with a long-term answer at quarterback only to have Andrew Luck retire after his second season as GM. He has weathered every unprecedented storm that has come his way and stayed true to his vision and process. I really respect that. On the other hand, during his tenure the Colts have failed to develop into a winner. He used a 2023 top 5 pick on a (so far) busted quarterback and only got another year at the helm in 2026 because the first 8 games last season were a whole lot of fun to watch. He should have been fired a season ago, but he’s still here, there’s no point crying about it with every other statement like so many Colts fans do. Hopefully the moves he made last offseason make sense once December rolls around. We’ll…
author: eboracum

title: Why Bill Parcells considers Jacoby Brissett to be like a son
summary: Bill Parcells has been a mentor to Jacoby Brissett since high school, guiding him through football and life decisions.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Twice a year since high school, Jacoby Brissett walked into Duffy's Sports Grill in Jupiter, Florida, and headed to the round booth in the corner for a lunchtime "Board of Directors" meeting.

 Except Brissett wasn't on the board of any organization, charity or company. And this certainly wasn't a conference room. His meetings were just three guys around a table talking about life and football -- which, for them, is largely one and the same.

 If there's a chairman of this mythical board, it's Pro Football Hall of Fame coach Bill Parcells, who named this biannual lunch that includes Brissett and his longtime friend and adviser Abe Elam.

 "We just sit and start talking," Brissett told ESPN.

 The conversation can range from Brissett starting at quarterback for the Arizona Cardinals  to Parcells' old team, the New York Giants , with whom he won two Super Bowls. The teams converge Sunday when the Giants host the Cardinals (1 p.m. ET, CBS).

 Parcells, who turned 85 in late August, spends his summers in upstate New York and winters on the east coast of Florida. He and Brissett will talk after Sunday's game just as they have after each of the first three games of the season. They meet when both are in Florida, even if it's not at Duffy's, which has closed.

 They'll talk football, but the relationship transcends sports. Parcells is one of the most important figures in the life of Brissett, 33. Their friendship spans nearly 20 years, back to when Parcells befriended Brissett's high school coach and started hanging around practices at William T. Dwyer High School in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. He became a mentor to Brissett, guiding him in finances, professionalism and, of course, football.

 In return, Parcells gained a willing pupil who parlayed his guidance into an 11-year NFL career. Brissett may not be the most talented QB Parcells has coached but lasting that long in the league is a testament to the intangibles that drew Parcells into the relationship.

 "I had three daughters; he's like a son," Parcells told ESPN. "That really is what the relationship is, in the respect that I look at it. And my job is just to try to guide and be direct as I can without being a nuisance and without badgering him and without doing anything or telling him, 'This is what you need to do. This is how you need to try to go forward in this business.'

 "And he's a very good listener, and he's done everything right in his career in terms of trying to prepare, getting ready physically, getting ready mentally. And he's been very good with his finances. He's a very good listener about that. And I'm just proud of him. I love him."

 

 Why Brissett believes he wouldn't be in the NFL if not for Parcells 

 Football wasn't Brissett's priority in high school. Far from it. In his mind, he was destined to play basketball. So, when Brissett met Parcells early in his high school career, Brissett didn't really know this older man coming to watch him practice.

 "The funny thing is, I hated football," Brissett said.

 "Then, as my high school coach started to explain the magnitude of who this guy was, obviously I watched football, but I never got super invested, and then over time, we spent so much time together, all the stories he tells me like, 'Hey, be expecting this and be prepared for this along your journey,' and stuff like that, and I'm like, the amount of times since he's been right to the point where I'm like, 'God dang, I got to start listening to this man.' His track record is pretty good."

 In Brissett, Parcells saw a kindred spirit, albeit one 50 years younger.

 "We both liked football and I could see he was a committed player," Parcells said. "He was anxious to learn and we talked not only about football, but a lot of different things in life."

 During lunch after the second time they met, Parcells told a teenage Brissett how they were similar.

 "He goes, 'You know, you're just like me. I'm white. You're Black. But we're the same person,'" Brissett recalled. "I'm like, 'How the hell are we the same? You're 65 and I'm 14.'"

 Once they began talking about themselves, their families, how much they love football, Brissett saw it.

 "I'm like, 'I got a lot in common with this old man.'"

 

 From then on, Parcells was there for Brissett.

 Whatever decision Brissett made throughout his career, Parcells supported. He encouraged Brissett to stick with football after high school, even though Brissett split snaps in high school with a quarterback who didn't play beyond their senior year. When Brissett decided to play quarterback at the University of Florida, Jeff Driskel , who was the top-rated prep quarterback the same year, was waiting for him in Gainesville. That didn't matter to Parcells. He didn't just tell Brissett it was the right decision. He reaffirmed it to him.

 "Here's what he's got going for him: First of all, he's very committed to the game. He loves the game. He loves playing. He's committed mentally, physically, and he just wants to be good at what he does," Parcells said. "And once you see that trait and you're a coach, you want to do everything you can to assist him."

 Even get down in the mud.

 One day while Brissett was preparing for the 2016 NFL combine, he was throwing routes on the field at his old high school in the rain, and Parcells, then 75, was on his knees in the mud snapping to Brissett.

 That memory still pops into Brissett's mind whenever Parcells texts the same thing after something good happens to Brissett: "I'm so proud of you. This is what we worked for."

 "I always tell him, 'Man, I would not be here if it wasn't for you,'" Brissett said. "I legit would probably be working at T-Mobile, no disrespect to T-Mobile, but something else.

 "Even to this day, he's still like, 'Send me videos of your workout. Let me see you in the gym in the offseason.' In the offseason, he goes, 'I want to make sure you're doing what you're supposed to be doing.' And he is legit. I sent him a video, he's telling me about my form. I'm like, 'You're a football coach, not a weightlifting coach.' But stuff like that. And it's like we've gotten to that point."

 Why Parcells persuaded Brissett to skip a rookie event 

 Not a conversation goes by, whether it's in person or on the phone, that Parcells doesn't remind Brissett to save his money. It doesn't happen once per conversation, but twice. It's typically the first thing Parcells brings up -- "You saving your money?" -- and the last thing he says before hanging up -- "Hey, make sure you keep saving your money."

 Brissett's money was an offseason storyline as he refused to participate in voluntary offseason OTAs and minicamp because of a contract dispute, and he held in -- attended but didn't participate -- during the mandatory minicamp in June. He reached agreement on July 26 on a $15.5 million guaranteed contract with a chance to make $21 million with incentives.

 Parcells has been a voice of reason and direction for Brissett, using a no-nonsense approach with nonstop support to get his message across. Parcells has spent years telling Brissett what he didn't want to hear but rather what he needed to hear, Elam said.

 It has helped Brissett become more self-aware and build self-confidence because he quickly realized that Parcells has been around long enough to know what's coming before it happens.

 During Brissett's rookie year with the Patriots, he was invited to the annual NFLPA rookie premiere in Los Angeles along with some teammates. The multiday event includes business seminars, networking and photo shoots. Parcells called Brissett and told him not to go. Brissett paused. He wanted to go. Parcells thought Brissett had a chance to play early that season while Tom Brady was suspended for four games because of his role in Deflategate.

 "It'll mean a lot if you stayed," Parcells told Brissett.

 

 Brissett listened. He stayed in Massachusetts, but it wasn't like he got extra time with…

title: The relationship between Bill Parcells and Jacoby Brissett
summary: Josh Weinfuss explains how close the bond is between Jacoby Brissett and Bill Parcells.

title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald ,  who unretired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach career top-five territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks heading into the season was 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the career list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White's.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 4 update 

 Watt kicked off things in Week 4 on "Thursday Night Football" in an impactful way. He had one sack, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery to move his total to 4.5 sacks on the season. 

 Week 3 update 

 There wasn't much movement on the list this week with only Mack (1) and Hunter (.5) recording sacks. Watt, Campbell, Hunter and Mack (in that order) now make up 25 to 28 on the all-time list. Along with Campbell, the three top active leaders -- Miller, Jordan and Garrett -- have yet to record a sack this season.  

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the career list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks (No. 2 in the NFL this season) and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded one sack apiece over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) made his  season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants after taking two years off. He finished with three tackles, one for a loss, but did not record a sack. 

 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: 2026 NFL trade deadline early look: Candidates to move, key teams, predictions
summary: Could the Cardinals listen on Marvin Harrison Jr. or Josh Sweat? Will the Bears or Raiders be active? Here's our way-too-early preview of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.
full_text:
The NFL's trade deadline is about five and a half weeks away. On one hand, that makes it a little bit early to be talking about who could get moved and where they could go. But on the other hand ... there were already two trades this week ! If the Vikings, Giants, Steelers and Cowboys don't think it's too early to talk trades, then neither do we.

 So, here's our annual trade deadline lookahead, complete with a list of 10 names who could be on the move for various reasons, five teams we think could be active in trade discussions and a few predictions thrown in at the end just for fun.

 Remember: The trade deadline is Nov. 10 (4 p.m. ET), which falls right after Week 9 as the league hits midseason. We don't know for sure which teams will be adding and which teams will be subtracting. A lot of what you'll read below comes with the appropriate disclaimers. If the Raiders keep winning, for example, it's more likely they add than subtract. If the Chargers keep losing, they're more likely to subtract than add. And so on. Nothing here is firm -- we are simply using conversations with team executives around the league to highlight some situations in which roster needs, team fit or contract situations might lead to activity. Let's begin with players to keep an eye on.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 10 players who could get traded 
 Five teams that could be adding 
 Five predictions for what will happen 

 
 

 10 players who could get traded before the Nov. 10 deadline 
 

 Marvin Harrison Jr ., WR, Arizona Cardinals 
 Harrison, the fourth pick of the 2024 draft, is tied for fifth on his own team in targets behind tight end Trey McBride , wide receivers Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne and rookie running back Jeremiyah Love. He has the same number of targets (nine) as  Tyler Allgeier , the team's No. 2 running back. Harrison has caught four passes for 73 yards in three games (after posting a 41-608-4 line in 2025).

 The perception of Harrison from people around the league is that he isn't a fit in an Arizona offense that prioritizes McBride as its top target, and that has led some teams to think he might be available. For their part, the Cardinals have given no indication that they are eager or even interested in trading Harrison. But if he's still an afterthought in the offense a month from now, there are plenty of teams that would be interested in taking a shot on his talent and making him a bigger part of their offense.

 
 

 

 Khalil Mack , Edge, Los Angeles Chargers 
 The Chargers being 0-3 is one of the big surprises of the early part of the season. They expected to be high-level contenders and therefore are not of the mindset to be moving players. If they turn it around and look like the team we expected, then no, I don't think they'd trade their beloved veteran edge rusher.

 But if they don't turn it around, and if they think they're slipping out of contention come early November, Mack could be appealing to a contending team looking to improve its pass rush for the stretch run. He signed for one year and $18 million this offseason, but $10 million of that was a signing bonus that has already been paid. So an acquiring team would be on the hook for only whatever remains of his $8 million salary at the time of the trade. Mack has two sacks through three games.

 
 

 Mason Rudolph , QB, Pittsburgh Steelers 
 As I stated in Wednesday's buzz file , I expect at least one more quarterback to get traded ahead of the deadline. The Vikings already dealt  J.J. McCarthy to the Giants earlier this week, but it's a position at which teams are always looking to improve (I guess unless we're talking about the three-deep Ben Johnson Bears). So I'm putting Rudolph in here as kind of an avatar.

 The Steelers have four quarterbacks on their roster -- 42-year-old starter Aaron Rodgers , second-year man Will Howard , rookie Drew Allar  and Rudolph. If something happens to Rodgers and he can't play, I believe Rudolph would take over. But if we get to early November and Rodgers is still healthy, the Steelers could get an offer that convinces them to move on from their longtime backup. That'd be especially true if, by then, they feel good about Howard and/or Allar as Rodgers' backups.

 
 

 Tony Pollard , RB, Tennessee Titans 
 The Titans have not looked good -- Pollard sort of has, rushing for 173 yards at 4.6 per carry. He's also 29 years old and making an affordable $6.74 million in the final year of his contract. Tennessee still has Tyjae Spears in the backfield, and the Titans drafted Penn State running back Nicholas Singleton in the fifth round of this year's draft.

 Running back is a position where teams endure significant attrition throughout the season, and Pollard is a veteran who could help fill a hole with a contender if the Titans fall out of contention as many expect. If he's healthy and not in Tennessee's long-term plans beyond this season, Pollard is the kind of player who could be on the move.

 
 

 

 Josh Sweat , Edge, Arizona Cardinals 
 Sweat has two years left on his contract, but none of the money beyond this season is guaranteed, and he did spend a chunk of the offseason in a contract dispute with the team . At one point, he reportedly requested a trade.

 I don't want to pick on the Cardinals, who have shown a great deal of fight under first-year head coach Mike LaFleur and could well be 2-2 after this weekend. But if they do tumble out of contention, that's not the kind of thing that makes veterans with contract gripes stop wanting out. Sweat is a Super Bowl champion who's not yet 30 and could be very interesting to pass-rush-needy teams at the deadline. He is without a sack so far in 2026, but he had 12 last season.

 
 

 Keisean Nixon , CB, Green Bay Packers 
 The Packers, like the Chargers, did not expect to have a losing record at this point (or probably any point) of the season. They're dealing with massive injury issues, particularly on the offensive line -- the type of thing that can make it very tough to right the ship after a difficult start. Nixon is 29 and in the final year of his contract. He has experience as a kick returner as well as cornerback, and an acquiring team would be on the hook for only a prorated portion of his $4.3 million 2026 salary.

 
 

 Josh Uche , Edge, Miami Dolphins 
 There are a lot of edge rushers on this list, but it's a spot at which teams are always looking for help. Uche signed a one-year, minimum deal with the Dolphins. He's a seven-year veteran who's playing well for a team in the first year of a significant rebuild. If the Dolphins get the opportunity to turn this signing into a useful draft pick, it's not at all hard to imagine them jumping on it.

 
 

 Daron Payne , DT, Washington Commanders 
 His contract voids at the end of the season, which will make him a free agent -- unless the Commanders extend him first. If they do that, feel free to scratch him right off this list. But if they don't, and if the Commanders aren't in the NFC East race by midseason, their 2018 first-round pick could be of interest to teams looking to fill holes along their defensive lines.

 If the Commanders aren't tumbling out of contention by November, they could also be the type of team that's looking to trade a veteran player for another, potentially dealing a guy who isn't part of their future for a player they believe could be. Or maybe they could look to strengthen a different position. There are a lot of ways the season can still go in Washington, but it might need to stay active in order to keep its playoff hopes alive.

 

 
 

 Jerry Jeudy , WR, Cleveland Browns 
 Jeudy is still only 27 years old, and he's signed through 2027. But the Browns' wide receiver corps has been taken over by rookies, and Jeudy might no longer fit squarely into the plans. He's owed about $23 million in salary and bonus for 2027, but it's not guaranteed, so an acquiring team wouldn't likely be deterred by that. He has two catches for 26…

title: Make pass interference reviewable? 17 NFL coaches are split
summary: It's been tried once before and some coaches want to bring it back, but others want to keep status quo.
full_text:
With 28 seconds left in the fourth quarter Sunday afternoon, Baltimore Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins batted away a pass from Dallas Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb near the goal line, making what many thought was a clutch defensive play. The Ravens led 31-28 at the time.

 Wiggins positioned himself in front of Lamb and might have intercepted the pass if not for his left arm getting interlocked behind him with Lamb's right arm.

 Then the flag hit the ground, and the blurred lines around arguably the NFL's most subjective call surfaced again. Wiggins was flagged 20 yards for defensive pass interference, and the Cowboys moved two yards away from the end zone for a potential go-ahead touchdown. They settled for a field goal.

 J.J. Watt, a former All-Pro defensive lineman and current CBS analyst, believed it was offensive pass interference. Gene Steratore, a former NFL referee and now a CBS rules analyst, also thought the penalty was against Lamb.

 The Ravens ultimately overcame the call to win 34-31, but the debate over how pass interference was officiated reignited.

 The week's Sunday night game poured more fuel on that fire when Los Angeles Rams cornerback Josh Wallace was called for DPI against the Denver Broncos ' Pat Bryant . Rams coach Sean McVay said Wednesday the league told the team the call was a mistake . The Broncos scored on the drive to take a 30-26 lead with 47 seconds left. That would be the final score.

 Pass interference is not subject to review by NFL rules. That wasn't the case in 2019 after an egregious missed DPI cost the New Orleans Saints the NFC Championship Game against the Rams the previous season. Overall, the NFL reviewed 101 pass interference calls or non-calls in 2019 and overturned 24. The league reversed its decision the following season and the call hasn't been reviewable since.

 

 "There's a human element to everything in this game," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "There are going to be times where calls are right and calls are wrong, and it is what it is."

 But not all coaches share that ambivalence. ESPN asked 17 NFL head coaches: What would be your thoughts about possibly bringing back challenges for defensive pass interference? Their answers varied, but in several, their responses were adamant.

 Here's what they said.

 

 

 Sean McVay, Los Angeles Rams 
 McVay is a member of the competition committee. 

 Those are things that I'll worry about at a later date. I'm interested in things that move us forward. Me spending any mental or emotional energy on what happened the other day doesn't do that.

 I think it's a subjective call. We've tried some of those things after the situation happened in our favor in 2018 and that opened up a can of worms, so I don't have a great answer for you on that note.

 

 Sean Payton, Denver Broncos 
 Payton is a member of the competition committee. 

 I said this the other day, the older you get in this, the wiser you get in this, you end up just not focusing on those things that are out of your control. You just hope when your career is over you're on the better end of those than not so better end.

 I think having watched [the competition committee] go through it, my guess would be not any time soon.

 

 Brian Schottenheimer,  Dallas Cowboys 
 Yeah, I think the league's learned that they can do a lot of things in a short period of time with the calls going to New York. So yeah, I wouldn't be opposed to that.

 

 

 Liam Coen, Jacksonville Jaguars 
 Coen was the assistant receivers coach for the Rams during the 2018 season, when no DPI was called against L.A.'s' Nickell Robey-Coleman after he leveled Saints WR Tommylee Lewis early (Payton was the Saints' head coach at the time). The play late in the fourth quarter of the NFC Championship Game enabled the Rams to advance to the Super Bowl. The NFL allowed for DPI challenges the following season. 

 Yes. Especially in critical moments, just make sure we get them really right and whatever it comes out to be, whatever the outcome is, it is what it is.

 And I've been on the other end of it, too, like the 2018 New Orleans playoff game. I've been on that end of it, too.

 And look, at the end of the day, you want it to just be fair. You just want it to be consistent and whatever the outcome is, if you've got to go live with the outcome, as Sean [McVay] mentioned. It's like we're not going to live in that and make an excuse for it. So whatever they decide, it is what it is. It's just in some of those moments, you just want the players to earn it. You want whatever team wins or loses the game, in my opinion, you just want it earned. You want it in the player's hands to win the game, not anybody else's.

 

 Kyle Shanahan, San Francisco 49ers 
 I thought it was good [in 2019], because I'm always, regardless of what happens, I just want them to get it right. Especially if you can see it on TV. It sucks to have to live with the wrong way when you're in the heat of battle on the field, which is what the challenge is for. So, I was excited when they made pass interference challengeable back then.

 And then after going through that year, I don't think I ever want it back because it got too much and there was too much ... and it just probably would be like challenging fouls in the NBA. It just gets a little hard. So probably not a fan of it anymore.

 

 Shane Steichen, Indianapolis Colts 
 It's a great question. I mean, sometimes you're on the flip side of it, where you don't want [the replay]. We've been on the other side of it, as you know, a couple years ago. It's happened to us, too. And, so, there's a lot of calls that happen in real time that are hard for these officials. Just being honest. You've got to make these split decisions just like players got to make decisions, coaches. And I think it's all part of it.

 I think it at the end of the day [it] kind of balances itself out, to be honest. If you look around the league, you probably go back to all the situations like, 'Oh, we got to win with one there. They got to win with one there.' And I think that's just part of the league and that's how it goes."

 

 Kevin O'Connell, Minnesota Vikings 
 O'Connell is a member of the competition committee. 

 I think it's a slippery slope. Look, the officials have a hard job. I know we can slow-mo something and see it a thousand frames per second or whatever. I've had a ton of conversations over the years in joint practices when we have those crews in, just trying to continue to learn the fundamentals. It's not just DPI and OPI. It's illegal contact. It's holding. It's why certain calls happen on certain plays versus DPI on another. And I think once you learn and continue to try to learn the fundamentals of it, you can understand they have a hard job to do.

 

 And offenses don't just stand there stagnant. There's motions, there's exchanges of receivers and all those things kind of weigh into where an official's eyes are at the beginning of a play versus the play going on and then ultimately the end of the play. So I do feel like they do the best job they can. I do feel like they don't have the luxury of slowing it down like that. I think when you do that, you're going to see a lot. You're going to see a lot both ways. You're going to see a lot of things that ... could change the dynamic, but not on the field, not from those officials.

 So I think we've tried it. I know we looked at it, being a part of the competition committee, just looking at the data on it and just what it looked like. I think they're going to continue to try to do the best job they can, but unfortunately some of those calls that come up, I think it's part of the game. Are you doing everything to coach the techniques and fundamentals on both sides? That's what [defensive coordinator Brian Flores] and I talk a lot about. Really good fundamentals and technique normally make those penalties or lack thereof be pretty apparent. It's when technique slips on one…

title: All-time rosters for 23 teams with multiple Super Bowls
summary: This was no small task, but 13 players ended up making more than one all-time SB roster.
full_text:
ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February 2027. We will count down to the big game with Super Bowl-centric stories every month. 

 Picking an all-time Super Bowl team for Super Bowls I-XL would be a difficult task, matching up players from different eras, under different rules and different schematics, but a lot of the names would be familiar and mostly Hall of Fame worthy.

 Picking an all-time Super Bowl team for each individual franchise is a little trickier.

 Twenty-three teams have played in multiple Super Bowls. Our goal was to come up with an all-time roster for each of those franchises, leaning toward the success those players had in the Super Bowls in which they played, regardless of the success of their overall career or in that particular season(s).

 As an example, Larry Brown was one of the Dallas Cowboys ' choices at cornerback, not Hall of Famer Deion Sanders .

 Why? Brown intercepted two passes in Super Bowl XXX and was named the game's Most Valuable Player.

 Across all of the 23 rosters, 13 players were selected for two franchises' all-time Super Bowl teams, including four former New England Patriots : QB  Tom Brady (Buccaneers), K  Adam Vinatieri (Colts), G  Joe Thuney (Chiefs) and TE  Rob Gronkowski (Buccaneers).

 Here are the selections made by our NFL Nation reporters:

 Jump to:

 CIN  | DAL  | DEN  | GB  |  IND 
 KC  |  LAR | LV | MIA  | MIN 
 NE  | NYG  | PHI  | PIT  | SF 
 SEA  |  TB  |  WSH 

 

 

 Atlanta Falcons 

 2 Super Bowls (0-2): XXXIII, LI  

 

 All-time Super Bowl roster:

 Defense

 MLB: Jessie Tuggle

 LCB: Robert Alford 
 SS: William White 
 FS: Keanu Neal 
 RCB: Ronnie Bradford

 

 Special teams 
 P: Matt Bosher 
 K: Matt Bryant 
 LS: Josh Harris 
 KR: Tim Dwight 
 PR: Eric Weems

 

 The Super Bowl LI team accounts for most of the selections given how potent the Falcons were on offense in that game despite the historic blowing of that 28-3 lead. Matt Ryan was 17-of-23 passing for 284 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions, outplaying his New England Patriots counterpart, Tom Brady. Julio Jones had 87 yards on four catches, Devonta Freeman ran for 75 yards and a touchdown, and Austin Hooper added a touchdown.

 Terance Mathis made a case for WR1 with seven catches for 85 yards and a touchdown in Super Bowl XXXIII, but it's hard to pick against Jones. The Super Bowl LI team led the way on defense, too. Grady Jarrett had three sacks, Robert Alford had a pick-six and Deion Jones was a standout. The Falcons had no sacks of John Elway in Super Bowl XXXIII, but Ronnie Bradford did intercept him. The easiest pick overall might have been Tim Dwight, who had 210 yards in kick returns in Super Bowl XXXIII, including a 94-yard touchdown. -- Marc Raimondi 

 

 

 Baltimore Ravens 

 2 Super Bowls (2-0): XXXV, XLVII  

 

 All-time Super Bowl roster:

 When it comes to the Ravens' two Super Bowl championship teams, it was nearly a clear-cut split considering the 2000 team was carried by Ray Lewis and defense and the 2012 one was led by Joe Flacco and the offense.

 The offensive players from the 2000 team who made the all-time Super Bowl team were left tackle Jonathan Ogden, who is in the Pro Football Hall of Fame; running back Jamal Lewis, who ran for 102 yards and a touchdown in the Super Bowl; tight end Shannon Sharpe, who delivered big plays throughout the postseason; and wide receiver Brandon Stokley, who scored the franchise's first touchdown in a Super Bowl.

 The defensive players from the 2012 team were middle linebacker Lewis, who was also the Super Bowl MVP in 2000; cornerback Jimmy Smith, who broke up a fourth-down pass in the final two minutes; and safety Ed Reed, who intercepted 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick in the second quarter. -- Jamison Hensley

 With all four of the Bills' Super Bowl appearances falling in one brief, snake-bitten span, this list reads more like a plausible re-creation of what the early 1990s Bills could've looked like on any given Sunday than a true Super Bowl all-star squad.

 Though this core group never hoisted a Lombardi Trophy, good individual performances shouldn't be overlooked. Take Don Beebe and Andre Reed's combined 39 catches for 494 yards and two scores and Thurman Thomas' 348 Super Bowl scrimmage yards. Or take Bruce Smith's two sacks and a safety paired with Jeff Wright's three sacks and 10 tackles.

 Maybe it's a backhanded compliment to Bills fans to even dare to include specialists on this list, but Steve Christie never actually missed a Super Bowl field goal attempt. -- Nick Suss

 Strictly based on Super Bowl performance, Jake Delhomme deserves the quarterback spot over Cam Newton. Delhomme threw for 323 yards and three touchdowns against the Patriots in SB XXXVIII, while Newton threw for 265 yards and an interception against the Broncos in SB 50. Both fumbled and lost the ball on the biggest stage, but Newton coughed up the ball twice, and Delhomme's QB rating (113.6) more than doubled Newton's mark (55.4).

 Elsewhere, Dan Morgan, who is currently the Panthers' general manager, notched 18 tackles in the Super Bowl XXXVIII loss. Kony Ealy produced three sacks, a forced fumble and an interception, while Reggie Howard got a pick of his own.

 Muhsin Muhammad, Steve Smith Sr. and Ricky Proehl all scored receiving touchdowns -- the only Panthers with TD catches in a Super Bowl -- and averaged more than 17 yards per reception. DeShaun Foster, who didn't start his Super Bowl game, produced more on four touches (52 total yards and a touchdown) than any other…

title: Tennessee Titans, Derrick Henry on different paths at the moment
summary: The running back has been on an upward trajectory since leaving Tennessee, while the Titans have followed a diverging path.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- There was once a time when the Tennessee Titans were among the final four teams remaining in the playoffs after the 2019 season.

 Although Ryan Tannehill 's ultra-efficient quarterback play sparked an unlikely run to the AFC Championship Game, it was Derrick Henry who was the catalyst for Tennessee. It was also Henry's image that was on network postseason advertisements along with Patrick Mahomes for the Kansas City Chiefs , Jimmy Garoppolo for the San Francisco 49ers , and Aaron Rodgers for the Green Bay Packers .

 Imagine that, a running back mixed in with three quarterbacks in a time when most teams featured pass-happy offensive attacks.

 So much has changed since then for the Titans -- and Henry.

 Henry's last game with the Titans was the 2023 season finale, a 20-16 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars . That game marked the end of an era, not just for Henry; it was the end of the road for Tannehill as well. Tennessee has a 6-31 record since Henry left in 2024, while Henry remains one of the game's best running backs -- just for the Baltimore Ravens . 

 Henry will get his first opportunity to face his former team when the Titans travel to the Ravens Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 "It's still like family there," Henry said Wednesday. "It's always love. But there ain't going to be much love on Sunday." 

 That's easy for Henry to say as he has been on an upward trajectory since he left Tennessee, while the Titans have followed more of a diverging path.

 
 Henry returned to the playoffs in his first season with the Ravens thanks in large part to his 1,921 rushing yards and 16 touchdowns. Baltimore has a 20-14 record since Henry signed.

 No team has lost more games than the Titans dating back to the start of the 2024 season, Henry's first year in Baltimore. Both at 9-28, the New York Jets and New York Giants are the next two franchises with the most. Ironically, both teams handed Tennessee a loss in 2026, contributing to the Titans' 0-3 record this season. 

 Henry and the Ravens are Super Bowl contenders, while the Titans are an early contender for the No.1 pick in the 2027 NFL draft .

 As Tennessee's rebuild continues, there has been a large amount of turnover.

 A coach or general manager in the Titans organization has been fired every year since 2022, starting with the firing of general manager Jon Robinson, who signed Henry to a four-year, $50 million contract extension in 2020. Ran Carthon replaced Robinson in 2023. Head coach Mike Vrabel was fired in 2024 after a 6-13 record and only one year with Carthon. 

 Titans controlling owner Amy Adams-Strunk wanted to implement a more modern offense that would be more reliant upon the passing game, so Carthon hired former  Cincinnati Bengals  offensive coordinator Brian Callahan to replace Vrabel.

 

 In 2024, Carthon, a former NFL running back himself, understood it was clear both Henry and the team needed to part ways, allowing Henry to pursue a championship while the Titans underwent a rebuilding process. 

 "I knew the writing was on the wall throughout that season and they were ready to move on," Henry said. "Good things don't last forever. So it was time for me to find a new home, and I knew what that home I wanted it to be and it was here [Baltimore]." 

 
 Tennessee attempted to replace Henry via free agency with former Dallas Cowboys running back Tony Pollard  in 2024 -- Pollard rushed for 1,079 yards and four touchdowns in his first season with the Titans, but the team finished tied with the Cleveland Browns and Giants for the worst record (3-13) in the league that year.

 Meanwhile, the Ravens made it to that postseason with Henry's 186 rushing yards and two touchdowns against the Pittsburgh Steelers pushing Baltimore to the divisional round, where they suffered a 27-25 loss to the Buffalo Bills .

 Carthon was quickly relieved of his duties in 2025 after two seasons. Mike Borgonzi took over for Carthon and selected Cam Ward with the No.1 overall pick. Callahan was fired after a 1-5 start, and the Titans finished with a 3-14 record last season in Ward's first year as a starter. While at the same time in Baltimore, Henry's 1,595 rushing yards and 16 touchdowns were the second most in each category in 2025. But the Ravens finished with an 8-9 record and missed the playoffs. Pollard's 1,082 rushing yards gave him his fourth consecutive season with 1,000 or more rushing yards, joining Henry as the only two backs to do so over the past four seasons.

 The six wins in Henry's final season in Tennessee would be welcomed by the current Titans, who have won that in total over the past two seasons and counting. The Titans have only won two games at Nissan Stadium since Henry's departure. That's a far cry from the "HEN-RY, HEN-RY" chants that broke out during home games in Henry's prime Titans years (2019-24). 

 "He was the face of the franchise for a while," Titans running back Julius Chestnut said of his former teammate. "The way he played. The way he runs, he's just angry, and it sprays off to other teammates. It makes you want to go harder."

 Ward was next in line to be the face of the franchise, but his 3-17 record in his first 20 games hasn't given much hope things will turn around any time soon.

 Take for example, the final offensive play of the Titans' 12-7 loss to the Giants last week as a microcosm of Ward's time in Tennessee. Ward stepped up in the pocket and scrambled to his left while being pursued by Giants linebacker Arvell Reese . With the game in the Titans' grasp, Ward had multiple options: run the ball, throw it out of bounds or throw it to the corner of the end zone, allowing Elic Ayomanor to make a play. Ward did neither as he tried to loft the ball over safety Jevon Holland 's head only to be intercepted and lose the game.

 Among 88 QBs who have debuted in Ward's career -- and started at least 20 games -- Ward ranks 81st in Total QBR (35.8).

 Ward is in need of a signature win, and going to Baltimore and beating the Ravens could be just that as Henry's and the Titans path converge once more.

 "[Henry's] still effective. The people around the building who've been here love him," Ward said.

title: NFL Week 4 betting guide: Analysis and top plays for Sunday's games
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 4 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: find betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

 From spreads and moneylines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 4.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jump to: 
 Bowen's Game of the Week  | Solak's plays  | Walder's props 

 

 

 Bowen's Game of the Week 

 New England Patriots at Buffalo Bills (-6.5, 48.5) 
1 p.m. ET on CBS, Highmark Stadium, Orchard Park, New York

 

 The Buffalo Bills , the AFC favorite to reach the Super Bowl, will host last season's AFC Super Bowl representative, the New England Patriots , in a matchup of AFC East rivals Sunday.

 The Patriots will need game plan answers on both sides of the ball to counter the Bills' high-scoring offense, and they'll have to create a more defined passing game without A.J. Brown  (ankle) on the field. I like the Bills to win and cover in this one, and in a divisional game with this level of coaching and familiarity, I'll take the under on the total. Let's check out both clubs, and I'll add some props at the end to play, too.

 

 When the Bills have the ball: In their Week 3 win over the Chargers, the Bills failed to control offensive tempo, and they turned the ball over. It happens in this league. But don't let one game change the narrative on an explosive Bills offense leading the NFL in scoring (33.7 PPG) and producing top-10 numbers in both passing and rushing. Quarterback Josh Allen will see heavy single-high coverage from New England (both man and zone), which creates opportunities for the Bills to scheme for crossing concepts and big-play throws on deep over routes, and they can also attack the seams with tight end Dalton Kincaid . The man matchup to watch to here is DJ Moore against Christian Gonzalez (shoulder), if the Patriots corner is up for the game. Best versus best.

 And let's not forget the offensive balance the Bills have with running back  James Cook III , who has produced back-to-back games with at least 135 yards rushing, against a New England defense allowing 4.8 YPC. The question I always have for teams versus Allen, given his dual-threat ability, is how much man coverage can you play? And what is your answer for Allen as a runner in the low red zone? Let's see how the Patriots counter, as Allen has rushed for two scores in all three games played this season. He's the league's ultimate difference-maker.

 When the Patriots have the ball: Quarterback Drake Maye has made some reckless decisions with the ball, throwing a league-high six interceptions and registering a 45.9 QBR (25th in the league). But I'm not going to put this all on Maye, as the Patriots' wide receiver group is lacking juice and matchup edges. With Brown on IR, who is the boundary X to win the one-on-ones? The tape shows us that the New England wideouts aren't creating separation at a high rate. The key here is for Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels to scheme more defined throws -- while having answers to pressure -- versus a Bills defense that has been more zone-heavy (65.9% of opponent dropbacks). Maye is going to see split-safety coverage. Lift the safeties here and create those middle-of-the-field voids for the quarterback to drive the ball.

 More importantly, the Patriots need to generate some run-game efficiency with Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson to get the Bills out of two-deep coverage. The Patriots are averaging 3.9 YPC  (20th in the league) with an explosive run rate of 8.2% (25th). No question on the numbers here. They are down. Let's see how McDaniels game-plans for Jim Leonhard and the Bills' new defensive scheme to get his QB rolling again. And it wouldn't surprise me if the Patriots try to muddy this one up with a ball control/play-action script.

 Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

 

 James Cook III rushing yards OVER 88.5 (-111) 

 As mentioned, Cook has rushed for 135-plus in two straight, and he's averaging 19.3 carries per game. Plus, Cook has 12 rushes of 10 or more yards this season. Take the steady volume and the explosive-play ability here.

 Hunter Henry receiving yards OVER 30.5 (-110) 

 Henry has topped the 31-yard mark just once this season, and he was held to just one reception in the Week 3 loss to Jacksonville. However, I see the tight end as an answer to the two-high zone coverage of the Bills. Henry can be the outlet for Maye, while also pressing the seams.

 DJ Moore receptions OVER 3.5 (-133) 

 The juice isn't friendly on this one, but that's a low reception total for Moore. In the two full games Moore has played (he left Week 2 early with an injury), he had at least five receptions in both. Look for the Bills to use motion to deploy Moore, getting him free access off the ball versus man coverage.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Detroit Lions -3.5 (-112) at Carolina Panthers 

 It's important to watch the forecast for this game as we get closer to kickoff. There's a good chance of rain showers Sunday night, and we know that Jared Goff 's performance as a passer can be impacted more by bad weather, given his smaller hands. But I still feel comfortable taking this bet at this number because of the Panthers' injury issues. Both starting cornerbacks are expected to miss this game, which all but precludes Carolina from playing man coverage against Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams . If the Panthers take a zone-heavy approach, expect Jahmyr Gibbs to run wild -- heck, expect Gibbs to run wild anyway, as the Panthers are giving up more rushing yards per game to running backs than any other defense. Have I mentioned the Panthers' passing defense is also among the league worst against tight ends?

 The Lions have Carolina outgunned offensively, and I'm not sure Bryce Young can keep scoring pace. Receiver Jalen Coker (quad) is questionable, three starting offensive linemen ( Ikem Ekwonu , Damien Lewis and Taylor Moton ) are out, and a key backup ( Monroe Freeling ) is in concussion protocol. Detroit's defense is extremely gettable through the air, but the Lions have enough pass rush power to generate sacks and turnovers such that the Panthers can't keep this shootout within one score.

 Los Angeles Rams -3 (-115) at Philadelphia Eagles 

 

 I would only take this line at -3 (up to -120) and not buy the hook, so move quickly here. DeVonta Smith missed practice Thursday with his hamstring injury, which officially moves him into the "seriously questionable" category as we approach Sunday. I already leaned to the Rams' side with a healthy Smith. If he can't go, the Eagles' receiver corps will feature Dontayvion Wicks , first-round rookie Makai Lemon and Hollywood Brown against the loaded Rams secondary. Remember, pass-catching tight end Dallas Goedert is also out with a knee injury.

 The Eagles' defense had a brutal night last Monday against the Chicago Bears ' passing attack, regularly suffering communication issues as the Bears sent receivers in motion. They get another motion-heavy passing attack in Sean McVay's Rams offense, which gets Puka Nacua back at a critical time -- at 1-2, the Rams need a road win to prevent the sirens from screaming in their Super Bowl-aspiring season. They also have a vengeance play here, as they gave up a big second-half lead to the Eagles last season ... then lost…

title: Fantasy football last-minute pickups for Week 4: Raymond, Allen, Waller among top options
summary: If injuries or tough matchups have you seeking help, Matt Bowen provides options at each key position.
full_text:
At various points during the fantasy football season, injuries, bye weeks and breaking news can cause you to need reinforcements for your fantasy lineup. Every Friday throughout the 2026 NFL season, Matt Bowen will offer some late-week pickup options at each of the primary fantasy positions to help fill those holes, with an emphasis on deeper leagues. 

 Because of that, this column will focus mostly on players rostered in fewer than 50% of ESPN leagues, with occasional exceptions. 

 Looking at the Week 4 NFL slate -- and the available players -- I'll start with the wide receiver position. I have two veteran pass catchers who are seeing consistent volume and producing solid fantasy numbers. There are options at quarterback, too, and one signal-caller could be getting his top target back. We'll also hit on the running backs in line to see an increased role due to injury, plus I have a tight end and a defense to get into lineups.

 

 Wide receivers 

 Kalif Raymond , Chicago Bears (48.4% rostered; vs. Jets) 

 The Bears haven't announced whether Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent will start at QB for the Week 4 home game versus the Jets, but either way I'm still pushing for Raymond based on his route deployment in Ben Johnson's offense. Raymond scored 21 points in the Week 3 win over the Eagles, and he has at least five receptions in all three games played this season. Raymond will see the ball as an outlet on crossers, sit routes and unders, plus he has the speed to create big plays (deep over routes and verticals). Raymond fits as a WR3 this week.

 Keenan Allen , Indianapolis Colts (46.6% rostered; vs. Commanders) 

 

 Allen is a fit for a Colts passing game missing its vertical element with Alec Pierce out with a heel injury. Allen can uncover or make himself available to the quarterback, which we saw in the Week 3 game versus Houston. Allen caught six of a season-high nine targets for 63 yards and a score (18.3 points). Allen has six receptions in two of three games played, and he gets a solid matchup in Week 4 against the Commanders. Managers can start Allen as a WR3.

 Dontayvion Wicks (44.7% rostered) and Makai Lemon , Philadelphia Eagles (47.6% rostered; vs. Rams) 

 DeVonta Smith (hamstring) has been downgraded to doubtful for Sunday's home game versus the Rams, so managers can pivot to Wicks or Lemon, as both should see a bump in target volume. Wicks scored 12 or more points in each of his first two games, with at least four targets in all three this season, while Lemon caught three of four targets for 29 yards in the Week 3 loss to the Bears. I'm really interested in seeing how Lemon performs with an expanded role. The rookie out of USC has the traits to win at the top of the route and he accelerates through the ball.

 Mack Hollins , New England Patriots (11.2% rostered; at Bills) 

 The Bills have been zone-heavy under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, and they play from a two-deep safety look on 49.2% of opponent dropbacks. That works for Hollins, as he has the coverage awareness to find open voids on short-to-intermediate throws. Hollins caught six of nine targets for 87 yards in the Week 3 loss to the Jaguars (14.7 points), and he has seen at least five targets in two of three games played. He's a deeper-league option this week.

 Malik Washington , Miami Dolphins (23.3% rostered; at Vikings) 

 You can take a shot on Washington because of his versatility and expanding role. Washington caught five of a season-high 10 targets for 56 yards in the Week 3 loss to the Chiefs, plus he had two carries for five yards from backfield alignments. Washington has seen five or more targets in all three games this season, with at least one rushing attempt in the past two. The Vikings' pressure defense will create conflict for quarterback Malik Willis and Miami's protection schemes, but that unit is giving up the 10th-most points per game to opposing wide receivers.

 

 Quarterbacks 
 

 Marcus Mariota , Washington Commanders (18.4% rostered; at Colts) 

 

 I didn't see Mariota scoring 20.42 points on the Seahawks defense in Week 3. The veteran quarterback delivered the ball with timing and location, finishing with 183 yards and three touchdown passes. While I would like to see Mariota deployed more on designed carries, there is a clear connection here with Terry McLaurin (six receptions, 77 yards, one touchdown in Week 3), and we can't pass on this matchup versus Indianapolis. The Colts are allowing 276 yards passing per game (third most). Mariota is a solid QB2 in Week 4, while  Jayden Daniels (elbow) misses his second straight game.

 C.J. Stroud , Houston Texans (37.0% rostered; vs. Cowboys) 

 The touchdown numbers are down for Stroud (three), but he is scoring 15.4 fantasy PPG, plus he has added 54 yards rushing this season. And this Texans pass game could get a major boost if wide receiver Nico Collins (hamstring) is back Sunday. I really like the matchup versus a Dallas defense allowing 23.5 fantasy PPG to opposing QBs (third most). If Collins is a go, you can start Stroud as a QB2 in superflex formats.

 Sam Darnold , Seattle Seahawks (50.9% rostered; vs. Chargers) 

 Darnold dropped 27.66 points on the Commanders in Week 3, his first game back after suffering a glute injury early in the Week 1 opener versus the Patriots. Darnold turned the ball over twice in Washington, but he finished with 379 yards and four touchdown throws. With an elite No. 1 option in Jaxon Smith-Njigba (135 yards receiving per game), Darnold should be viewed as a quality QB2 this week versus a Chargers defense ranked 15th against opposing QBs.

 

 Running backs 
 

 Keaton Mitchell , Los Angeles Chargers (18.4% rostered; at Seahawks) 

 Mitchell had a season-high 11 touches in the Week 3 game versus Buffalo, finishing with 47 total yards and a touchdown, good for 13.7 points. We know he's an explosive change-of-pace runner behind Omarion Hampton (15 carries in Week 3), plus he can be schemed in the pass game. Mitchell has an ankle injury that we need to monitor, but if he's good to go this week, he has value as a flex in deeper leagues.

 Kendre Miller , New Orleans Saints (15.0% rostered; at Falcons) 

 

 Travis Etienne Jr . (hamstring, IR) is out for the forseeable future, so Miller should be back in the fold, sharing touches with Alvin Kamara in the Saints backfield. Miller saw six touches last week, and he had nine carries for 30 yards and a touchdown (on a low red zone attempt) in Week 1. I don't see a ton of upside here due to Kamara's usage in the game plan, plus the Falcons are allowing only 12.8 fantasy PPG to opposing running backs. But if you need to find an option in a deeper league, Miller will see the ball.

 Jaylen Wright , Miami Dolphins (23.3% rostered; vs. Vikings) 

 With De'Von Achane  (ACL) out for the season, Ollie Gordon II and Wright move into prominent roles in the Miami backfield. Gordon fits as the early-down runner with north/south traits, while Wright has the speed and traits to provide more perimeter/receiving upside. Wright has limited usage this season (three carries), but he did have two games of 12 or more points in 2025. It's a tough matchup against a Minnesota defense that ranks fourth versus running backs, so Wright should be a deeper-league option only.

 Isaiah Davis , New York Jets (7.4% rostered; at Bears) 

 Breece Hall (thigh) is out for this week, which moves Braelon Allen into the No. 1 role, while also opening the door for Davis to see work. Davis has yet to register a carry this season, but he averaged 5.5 YPC last season, posting three games with 10 or more points. He's a deeper-league flier who could produce some numbers against a Bears defense allowing 4.9 YPC.

 

 Tight end 
 

 Darren Waller , Carolina Panthers (26.3% rostered; vs. Lions) 

 Waller caught five of a season-high eight targets for 51 yards last week against the Browns, and he now has double-digit points in back-to-back games. With his increase…

title: Colts vs. Commanders, NFL London preview: ESPN experts on key players, matchups and predictions
summary: The NFL rolls into London this begin with a clash between the Indianapolis Colts and the Washington Commanders -- so we asked ESPN reporters Stephen Holder and John Keim for a preview.
full_text:
The NFL rolls into the United Kingdom this Sunday as the London Games begin with a clash between the Indianapolis Colts and the Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Ahead of the game, ESPN asked Colts reporter Stephen Holder and Commanders reporter John Keim to assess their respective teams, the players UK fans should watch and where Sunday's matchup could be won and lost... 

 

 How would you sum up the season so far? 
 

 SH:  It's been a bit of a struggle. The Colts' early-season schedule was not favourable and that resulted in two consecutive losses to the Ravens and Chiefs to begin the season. Last Sunday's win against the Texans was much needed, but the Colts' offense is feeling the loss of star receiver Alec Pierce , who will be out of the lineup for at least several weeks with a heel injury. There are also questions about the Colts' defense, which was embarrassed in its first two games.

 -  NFL International Games: Schedule, UK times for matches in London, more 
 -  Colts vs. Commanders: NFL London kick-off time, how to watch in UK 

 

 JK: Injury filled. Again. Washington was devastated by injuries in 2025 and it was one reason the team stumbled to a 5-12 season. Already this year, they will have played two games with seven players projected as starters when camp opened. All but one  -- left tackle Laremy Tunsil -- are expected back soon. Considering that, they're fortunate to be 1-2 after opening at Philadelphia, at Dallas and then home vs. Seattle. The Commanders are without their top players at: quarterback, left tackle, cornerback, linebacker, safety and tight end. They're forced to use a linebacker who was fifth on the depth chart entering the season ( Kain Medrano ).

 What's the biggest thing we've learned about this team that we didn't know coming into the season? 
 

 SH:  It's taking longer than hoped for some of the new additions on defense to make an impact. The Colts changed five of their 11 starting players on defense this season, and that has proven to be a difficult transition. Whether it all works as designed is still an open question as we are just three games into the season.

 

 JK: Their run defense is excellent. Washington had hoped it would improve in this area, but that was the case each of the last two years as well but it never materialised. From 2024-25, the Commanders ranked 30th in rushing yards allowed and 26th in yards per carry. But the defensive line -- Javon Kinlaw , Tim Settle and Daron Payne -- has been excellent and the linebackers speed has been a big factor as well. Odafe Oweh earned a big contract because he can rush the passer, but he's been terrific at setting the edge.

 

 

 What's the mood around the team about travelling to London? 
 

 SH:  The Colts are treating this like most any other game. Spirits are good because they won their last game, their first win this season. But the Colts have been adamant about their policy of traveling late in the week for their European games, as they have done in each of their three trips to the continent. The Colts' plan was to fly Thursday night and arrive in London on Friday morning. They will then eat, relax and get acclimated before holding a short practice on Friday afternoon.

 

 JK: Upbeat. However, while they were pleased with the win over Seattle, the players and coach Dan Quinn emphasised that it was just one game and that they had areas to correct -- if they want to build on the win. So while the win over Seattle made the flight to London much better, they did not view it as "we've arrived" but want to use it as a steppingstone, as quarterback Marcus Mariota said. And that's why numerous players harped on what they could do better to make sure one win leads to another.

 

 Who's been the standout player so far -- and who should UK fans watch out for? 
 

 SH:  Running back Jonathan Taylor has picked up where he left off last season, when he was one of the top runners in the NFL. But he will draw more attention from defenses in the coming weeks because the absence of Pierce allows opponents to focus more on run defense. Washington has found success defending runners in the past two games, so it will be interesting to see which team wins in this particular subplot.

 

 JK: Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles . He's far from a finished product, but the seventh overall pick already has made an impact. With  Frankie Luvu  sidelined, he's responsible for relaying the plays into the huddle and he's adept at communicating before the snap as well. He already has an interception and a forced fumble as well as a sack. He accomplished something no other rookie has done for Washington: record an interception, a forced fumble and multiple passes defensed in the same game. His speed has made a big difference in coverage and his ability to chase ballcarriers. He'll have to develop coming downhill and taking on blockers, but for now he's playing fast enough -- and the line is helping enough -- to avoid them.

 

 What's the biggest concern around the team heading into this game? 
 

 SH:  The Colts were yielding a historic amount of yardage in their first two games, leaving them statistically as the worst defense in the NFL. The 417.3 yards per game the Colts are allowing, on average, from opponents is well below the NFL average of 329.5. While the Colts made noticeable strides in their win against Houston last Sunday, it remains to seen whether they can sustain that momentum.

 

 JK: Health. But we already covered that above. Their depth will continue to be tested until more starters return over the next couple weeks. That's obvious so let's take a look at something else: the pass coverage. Indianapolis does not have a dynamic passing attack -- quarterback Daniel Jones ranks 18th in number of pass attempts of 15 air yards or more and only has a 56.6 passer rating on such throws. But the Commanders' weakness has been coverage; they've allowed the sixth most passing yards and the second most passing touchdowns.

 Where do you think Sunday's game will be won and lost? 

 

 SH:  Neither defensive unit in this game has shown itself to be reliably good. Each is yielding more than 30 points per game. What this game likely will hinge on is the respective quarterbacks' ability to exploit the opposing defense. Jones has a slight edge in this area in my mind.

 

 JK: I'll say the ground game. The Colts have two outstanding corners in Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward to contend with Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs . But they rank 28th in yards per carry allowed. The Commanders have remained devoted to running -- with the fourth most attempts despite being only 16th in yards per carry. But they will stick with it, using both Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White . If Washington's defense has been excellent vs. the run, with 27 of 64 carries going for two yards or less -- but if the Commanders continue stopping the run they must have better lane discipline when rushing Jones.

 Who wins and why? 
 

 SH:  I'm picking the Colts by a slim margin. My rationale: If the Colts star cornerbacks Gardner and Ward can limit Washington's receivers -- the Colts believe them to be the strength of their team -- it will position the Colts to prevail. But that's a matchup Indianapolis has to win to get the victory.

 

 JK: I was afraid you'd ask this question. This is a toss-up game; two 1-2 teams who faced a tough early schedule. I'll go with Washington and the ability to control the ground game; the key will be whether they can limit explosive pass plays. Mariota showed a tonne of poise and calmness in the pocket last week. This is a massive game for Washington: Can it build off a terrific win? We'll bet that they will, but the confidence isn't high because of their health and the teams are fairly equal.
